commits.subject: Fix --fwhole-program typo blocking release builds (#135)
commits.body:
g++ only recognizes the single-dash GCC spelling -fwhole-program;
the double-dash form was rejected as an unrecognized option, so any
'scons release=1' build failed at the final link step.

commits.subject: Complete translations for ar, de, eo, es, fa, fi, fr, nl, pl, ru, zh-cn; fix dk encoding and hu duplication (#133)
commits.body:
* Fix mojibake in Danish translations

One line in texts.dk.txt (Tilføj genvejstast / Add shortcut key) had
a single byte saved as Latin-1 instead of UTF-8, the encoding every
other translation file and the engine's text rendering (TTF_RenderUTF8_Blended)
uses. Rest of the file was already valid UTF-8.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Deduplicate texts.hu.txt

The file had accumulated up to 3 copies of many key/value pairs
(1757 entries for 603 unique keys, 988 of them blank), which is why
check_translations.py reported more untranslated keys than the game
has strings. Deduplicated to one entry per key, keeping the first
non-blank translation seen.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Complete translations for ar, de, eo, es, fa, fi, fr, nl, pl, ru, zh-cn

Fills in every key that was missing or blank relative to
texts.keys.txt / texts.en.txt (excluding the handful of 'explanation 2'
keys that are legitimately blank in English too), and flips off the
incomplete marker in texts.incomplete.txt for the languages that are
now fully translated (ar, de, eo, es, fa, fi, pl -- fr/nl/ru/zh-cn were
already unmarked and just needed top-up).

zh-cn's marker is left as-is: the bundled data/fonts/sans.ttf has no
CJK glyphs, so Chinese still renders as tofu regardless of translation
completeness.

texts.it.txt is flipped *on* (now correctly flagged incomplete, 123
of 602 real keys still missing) since it wasn't previously flagged
despite the gap; completing it is left for a follow-up.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Show a language code instead of tofu when its font glyphs are missing

The language picker showed a language's name in its own script, e.g.
Chinese. data/fonts/sans.ttf has no CJK glyphs, so this rendered as a
row of unreadable boxes for Chinese entries -- for every player, not
just non-Chinese ones, since SDL_ttf only draws from the one bundled
font file and does no system font-fallback of its own.

Font::hasGlyphsFor() (TrueTypeFont's real implementation checks each
codepoint via TTF_GlyphIsProvided32, other Font subclasses default to
assuming full coverage) lets the language list check before using a
name's own glyphs; when they're missing it falls back to that
language's (always-Latin) [language-code] value instead, e.g.
'zh-cn - missing font'.

Also fixes texts.zh-cn.txt's own [language-code], which incorrectly
held 'zh-tw' (copy-paste from the neighboring entry) -- StringTable
uses this value to resolve the saved language setting back to an
index, so this also silently broke restoring a saved 'zh-cn' choice.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Tighten a few translations that ran noticeably longer than English

Leo flagged translation length as a UI-overflow risk. Checked byte
length of every string I added against its English source: most
translations run 0-30% longer than English (normal for Romance/
Germanic languages), but a handful were 1.6-2.4x, mostly toggle
labels and buttons where that's more likely to actually overflow.
Shortened those:
- fr: 'watching:', 'show flags', 'show areas', 'watch again' to
  single-word/short-phrase forms; 'save replay' to match the verb
  ('Sauvegarder') the pre-existing 'save map' string already uses,
  instead of the shorter but inconsistent 'Sauver' I'd first used.
- es: 'the replays' (dropped article, matching how the pre-existing
  '[the maps]' -> 'Mapas' already drops it), 'replay ended',
  'Prestige Score'.
- de: 'show areas'/'show flags' to noun-only, dropping 'anzeigen'.

Left a few as-is on purpose: de's flag-related error strings match
the length of the pre-existing building/fruit variants of the same
message (consistency over brevity), and eo/fi's one long string each
reflects normal agglutinative-language compounding rather than a
verbose word choice.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

the FSF's pre-2005 mailing address. Replace it with
`// SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-3.0-or-later` followed by the file's

commits.subject: Connect the end-game chart segments end to end (#144)
commits.body:
Each chart segment ran from (px+1, previous value) to (px, new value),
so consecutive segments never shared an endpoint: at every column
boundary the curve jumped by one sample. Inside a 1 px column at 1:1
that is invisible, but with fullscreen scaling each column is several
pixels wide and steep slopes render as a row of disconnected dashes.
Draw from (px, previous value) to (px+1, new value).

Co-authored-by: Junior <junior-agent@noreply>

commits.subject: Remove leaked forbidden zone when a building dies awaiting upgrade room (#149)
commits.body:
When a building enters WAITING_FOR_CONSTRUCTION_ROOM for an upgrade,
addForbiddenZoneToUpgradeArea stamps the owning team's forbidden bit over
the would-be upgraded footprint. The two normal exits from that state
(tryToBuildingSiteRoom finding room, cancelConstruction) remove the zone,
but Building::kill() -- reached when the building is shot or beaten to
0 hp mid-wait -- did not, leaving the forbidden bits set forever and
corrupting the owning team's pathfinding over that area.

kill() now calls removeForbiddenZoneFromUpgradeArea() for that exact
state before clearing the building's tiles, so the subsequent gradient
rebuilds in kill() see the corrected zone. The zone is only ever stamped
for UPGRADE (never REPAIR), so the narrow conditional mirrors the add
site exactly.

Ported from PR #129 (feat/ai-trainer-support), original commit 7a61c299, adapted to master's file layout.

Co-authored-by: Junior <junior-agent@noreply>

commits.subject: Building: fix latent setBuilding(decLeft, decLeft) typo in tryToBuildingSiteRoom (#150)
commits.body:
The clear-old-footprint call in `tryToBuildingSiteRoom` passed
`type->decLeft, type->decLeft` for the rectangle's width and height.
`decLeft` is a negative centering offset (-1 or -2 in current data),
so `setBuilding`'s loops `for (i=y; i<y+(-1); i++)` ran zero
iterations — the call was a silent no-op.

The bug never manifested because the immediately following call
stamps the new (larger or same-sized) footprint with the same gid,
and every level of every current building is calibrated so the new
footprint is a centered superset of the old. Repair targets the
same-size building site (no shrink), upgrades grow outward from a
shared midpoint. Either way the would-be-stale tiles get re-stamped
correctly by line 323.

Match the pattern used in `cancelConstruction` (Construction.cpp:227)
and `kill` (Misc.cpp:85): pass `type->width, type->height`. Removes a
footgun for any future asymmetric upgrade or modder-added building
with a non-centered shape.

Behavior bit-identical for current data; checksum unchanged.

Ported from PR #129 (feat/ai-trainer-support), original commit 89f342e9, adapted to master's file layout.

Co-authored-by: Junior <junior-agent@noreply>

commits.subject: Fix stale building and unit selection when cycling (#158)
commits.body:
* iterateSelection: guard stale selection.building before deref

The BUILDING_SELECTION branch read selBuild->gid before its assert(selBuild)
null check, so a NULL selection cache (selection.building can stale past a
building's destruction -- onBuildingDestroyed only clears
game.selectedBuilding, and checkSelection runs at draw time, not before the
next keypress) crashed on the deref. Asserts also aren't stripped in glob2
release builds but would abort() rather than no-op the keypress; replace
both asserts with an early return so a stale selection cycle is a silent
no-op.

Ported from PR #129 (feat/ai-trainer-support), original commit
0249dd34fe5acea4c0551fde88835783f95ce921 by Kyle.

* Link selection regression against real client code

commits.subject: Map editor: only remove ressources the painted terrain no longer allows (#140)
commits.body:
* Map editor: only remove ressources the painted terrain no longer allows

Painting sand or water cleared every ressource in a square around the
cell, three wide for sand and five for water. A tile is drawn from the
undermap corners at (x..x+1, y..y+1), so the cell painted at (x, y)
changes the tiles from (x-1, y-1) to (x, y); the square, centred on the
cell, also cleared the column east and the row south of the new sand,
which stayed grass and lost their trees.

The terrain is painted first and Map::removeUnallowedRessources then
drops, over the tiles a stroke can change, only the ressources whose
terrain no longer matches, the same test setRessource applies when the
editor places one. Grass stays the brush that clears: it bares the
tiles the cell touches, and no longer the column and row beyond them.

* iterateSelection: guard stale selection.building before deref

The BUILDING_SELECTION branch read selBuild->gid before its assert(selBuild)
null check, so a NULL selection cache (selection.building can stale past a
building's destruction -- onBuildingDestroyed only clears
game.selectedBuilding, and checkSelection runs at draw time, not before the
next keypress) crashed on the deref. Asserts also aren't stripped in glob2
release builds but would abort() rather than no-op the keypress; replace
both asserts with an early return so a stale selection cycle is a silent
no-op.

Ported from PR #129 (feat/ai-trainer-support), original commit
0249dd34fe5acea4c0551fde88835783f95ce921 by Kyle.

* Validate live selection before cycling cached entities

* Link selection regression against real client code

* Exercise terrain resource preservation across brush overlaps and wrapped map edges

* Keep the merged harness instructions once and document both top-level targets

commits.subject: Preserve readiness and verify lobby slot compaction (#152)
commits.body:
* Map editor: only remove ressources the painted terrain no longer allows

Painting sand or water cleared every ressource in a square around the
cell, three wide for sand and five for water. A tile is drawn from the
undermap corners at (x..x+1, y..y+1), so the cell painted at (x, y)
changes the tiles from (x-1, y-1) to (x, y); the square, centred on the
cell, also cleared the column east and the row south of the new sand,
which stayed grass and lost their trees.

The terrain is painted first and Map::removeUnallowedRessources then
drops, over the tiles a stroke can change, only the ressources whose
terrain no longer matches, the same test setRessource applies when the
editor places one. Grass stays the brush that clears: it bares the
tiles the cell touches, and no longer the column and row beyond them.

* NetGamePlayerManager: fix wrong-direction shift in slot compaction

removePlayer's manual slot-compaction was setting numberMask via
`1u >> bp.number` (right-shift), which always yields 0. The canonical
setter at BasePlayer::setNumber uses `1 << number`. Route through
setNumber instead of duplicating the bit-twiddling, so the same typo
can't reappear.

Effect was benign in practice — numberMask is never consumed as a
real bitmask anywhere; its only consumer is BasePlayer::checkSum,
and the wrong value was consistent across all peers (server-
authoritative GameHeader). But the field travels in save files and
the network checksum, and a future use of numberMask as an actual
mask would have silently observed 0 for any compacted slot.

Also drops an unused #include "YOGServerGame.h" flagged by clangd.

Ported from PR #129 (feat/ai-trainer-support), original commit 44947adc, adapted to master's file layout.

* iterateSelection: guard stale selection.building before deref

The BUILDING_SELECTION branch read selBuild->gid before its assert(selBuild)
null check, so a NULL selection cache (selection.building can stale past a
building's destruction -- onBuildingDestroyed only clears
game.selectedBuilding, and checkSelection runs at draw time, not before the
next keypress) crashed on the deref. Asserts also aren't stripped in glob2
release builds but would abort() rather than no-op the keypress; replace
both asserts with an early return so a stale selection cycle is a silent
no-op.

Ported from PR #129 (feat/ai-trainer-support), original commit
0249dd34fe5acea4c0551fde88835783f95ce921 by Kyle.

* Validate live selection before cycling cached entities

* Link selection regression against real client code

* Exercise terrain resource preservation across brush overlaps and wrapped map edges

* Keep the merged harness instructions once and document both top-level targets

* Preserve survivor readiness when compacting lobby player slots

commits.subject: Letterbox the fullscreen scale instead of stretching it (#162)
commits.body:
* Letterbox the fullscreen scale instead of stretching it

When the logical resolution's aspect ratio doesn't match the window/desktop's, both the GL viewport and the software SDL_BlitScaled fullscreen paths stretched the logical rect to fill the window non-uniformly, squashing circles (button end-caps, cursors) into ellipses.

Scale both axes by the same factor (the smaller of the two, as drawableScale() already computed for line width and cursor scaling) and center the result, leaving black bars on the long axis instead of distorting. Apply the matching offset to windowToLogical() and setClipRect()'s glScissor so clicks and clipping still line up with what's drawn.

* Keep letterboxed screen captures in logical coordinates and verify both renderers

* Avoid invalidating the unchanged SDL window surface in the aspect test

commits.subject: Fix spurious scons "Two different environments" warnings (#172)
commits.body:
* src: stop double-compiling savegame-safety-test objects under a second env

savegame_env (a Clone() of local with tweaked LINKFLAGS/LIBS) was being
handed the raw source_files list, so scons re-registered every shared
object (BuildingUtils.o, Bullet.o, Campaign.o, ...) as built by a second
Environment instance, on top of the one already registered by local.Program()
for the client build and the other test harnesses. Same compile action,
different Environment object -> "Two different environments were specified
for target ..." warning per file.

Compile the shared sources through local.Object() first (the same env every
other target here uses) and only apply savegame_env at the link step, where
the LINKFLAGS/LIBS override actually matters.

Verified: clean 'scons -j4' and 'scons -j4 server=1' builds, plus every
test/*-test alias, produce zero 'Two different environments' warnings and
link successfully (glob2, glob2-server, SavegameSafetyHarness,
GameGUISelectionHarness, TerrainResourcesHarness, LANSessionHarness,
game-speed-tests, BuildingFootprintHarness, EnteringUnitSaveHarness).

commits.subject: Map editor: only remove units and buildings the painted terrain no longer carries (#171)
commits.body:
* Map editor: only remove units and buildings the painted terrain no longer carries

A terrain stroke paints the undermap corner between tiles x-1 and x, so
a cell changes the tiles (x-1..x); with the sand fringe grass and water
strokes reach (x-2..x+1). The stroke then cleared every unit and
building in a square centred on the cell, three wide for grass and five
for water, which reaches one tile further east and south than west and
north: a swarm two tiles east of the cursor vanished, the same swarm two
tiles west stayed.

Game::removeUnallowedUnitsAndBuildings drops, over the tiles a stroke
can change, the buildings whose tile is no longer grass and the ground
units on open water that cannot swim, the tests the editor applies when
it places them. Grass stays the brush that clears: it empties the four
tiles the cursor square covers, and nothing beyond them.

removeUnitAndBuildingAndFlags read the air unit for DEL_GROUND_UNIT and
the ground unit for DEL_AIR_UNIT; every caller passed both flags, so
nothing noticed. The flags now name the layer they clear. The new
caller spells out the size overload: a lone enumerator promotes to int
and would otherwise select that overload as the size, with the default
flags that clear everything.

The terrain harness gains the entity half of the oracle: a swarm, a
walker and an explorer around 300 single-cell strokes of each terrain,
a west/east mirror check, and a four-cell water stroke that drowns the
walker and keeps the explorer.

* Exercise terrain entity edits with valid game ownership and wrapped fixtures

commits.subject: Clamp ally-team widget index in the map editor's teams editor
commits.body:
The teams editor converted the header's 1-based ally-team number to a
0-based widget index by bare subtraction. A header carrying 0, or a
value above the map's team count, produced an index outside the rows
the widget was populated with; MultiTextButton::setIndex stores the
index unsigned and looks it up with vector::at, so the dialog threw
std::out_of_range and crashed on open.

The custom-game options screen had already fixed the same defect with
a file-local clamp helper. Promote that helper to a shared header-only
AllyTeamWidgetIndex.h and use it at both sites. Well-formed values
still map to value - 1, so nothing written back changes; only headers
that previously threw now show ally team 1.

Also name the teams editor's widget return-code bases (player-active,
color, AI selector, ally team) instead of hand-typing 100/200/300/400
at nine sites, and document generateGameHeader's inverse mapping.

Verified: standalone driver tests/ally_team_widget_index_test.cpp
passes; cpp-refactor.replay byte-identical after the change.

commits.subject: Value-initialize the settings screen's flag-default widget arrays
commits.body:
flagRadii, flagRadiusTexts and flagRadiusGroupNumbers were the only
members of the Building Defaults tab left out of the constructor's
initializer list. Their unitRatio* counterparts are already covered --
unitRatioGroupNumbers by the initializer list, unitRatios and
unitRatioTexts by the nulling loop at the top of buildBuildingDefaultsTab
-- so the flag arrays were the odd ones out.

This is hardening rather than a bug fix: buildFlagsGroup() populates all
three slots unconditionally during construction, and every reader runs
from onAction or onGroupActivated, so no read ever preceded a write. But
the read sites null-check flagRadii and flagRadiusTexts anyway, which
reads as a signal that empty slots occur. They don't. Document the
invariant at the declaration so that asymmetry with the genuinely sparse
unitRatios grid isn't mistaken for a missing case.

No behavior change; the settings screen is not on the simulation path.
Verified byte-equal against tests/baselines/cpp-refactor.replay.

commits.subject: Replace the chamfer gradients with weighted per-swim-class fields
commits.body:
Pathfinding gradients become Uint16 fields built by a bucket-queue
Dijkstra: a cardinal step costs 10, a diagonal 14, and water is charged at
the unit's walk/swim ratio, bucketed into swim classes. Every gradient
(resources, forbidden, guard and clear areas, buildings) is kept per swim
class and built the first time a unit of that class asks for it.

Units step to the neighbour whose value minus the step cost is highest,
which also removes the 5x5 minigrad and the 32x32 local building grids:
a building has one full-map gradient per class, rebuilt when the map

commits.subject: Cache compilation in CI with ccache (#179)
commits.body:
* Cache compilation in CI with ccache

CI rebuilds every object from scratch on each of the four builds a run
performs, across two container images. Wrapping the compilers in ccache
lets the compiles hit a content-addressed store instead.

Only ccache's store is cached. The build/ tree and .sconsign.dblite stay
out of it: those are incremental state whose correctness depends on
scons's dependency scanner having recorded every input, and it does not
record all of them -- DET_INIT is read straight from the environment,
and the Configure results in config.h and options_cache.py are not
tracked either. Persisting that across runs is how a stale object
survives a source change. ccache re-hashes the source, every header it
includes by content, the compiler binary and the full command line on
every compile, so scons still rebuilds its dependency graph from a
fresh checkout each run and only the individual compiles are reused.

CCACHE_SLOPPINESS is left unset for the same reason: include_file_mtime
and include_file_ctime would trade content hashing for timestamps, and
time_macros would let ccache serve a stale __DATE__/__TIME__ banner for
GlobalContainerArgs.cpp. CCACHE_COMPILERCHECK=content covers a g++ point
release landing inside a base image.

Two tripwires: the per-run statistics are printed, so a change to a
widely included header that still shows near-total direct hits is
visible, and the existing harnesses already run against the produced
binaries.

Only master writes the cache, and it writes whenever the compiles ran,
including runs a later test step failed -- the entries are
content-addressed, so a failing test says nothing about whether the
objects are the right objects.

Enabled by CCACHE=1 in the environment rather than a scons option, so it
cannot stick in options_cache.py. Windows is not covered.

* Handle cache reruns and manual warming; test compiler integration

commits.subject: Map: fix immobile-unit bookkeeping and refresh gradients on painted forbidden area (#187)
commits.body:
* Map: fix immobile-unit bookkeeping in local gradients

Map::setSize filled immobileUnits with 0, which is team 0's marker; the
"no unit here" sentinel is IMMOBILE_UNIT_NONE, as MapIO uses on load. On
any freshly built map (random maps, the editor, harnesses) every free
tile counted as blocked by an immobile unit, the local gradient marked
the whole window forbidden, the building was declared unreachable, and
every unit fell through to the full-map global gradient. Loaded maps
were unaffected.

Map::updateLocalGradient indexed immobileUnits with the local-window
index instead of the map index used for cases[] on the line above and
by MapGradientBuilding.cpp, so an immobile unit blocked whichever window
tile shared its number with the unit's map index, never its own tile.

test/ImmobileUnitGradientHarness.cpp links the real engine on a 64x64
map and checks both: a fresh map has no immobile unit and reachable
local gradients, and a marked unit blocks exactly its own tile. Each
scenario fails on its unfixed line.

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

* Refresh building gradients when forbidden area is painted

Game::executeAlterForbidden dropped the team's building gradients only
when area was erased. After a paint, every gradient still led through
the tiles just closed; units kept walking toward a former gap until one
of them reached the wall and the near-field check refused the step, and
the global gradient is recomputed at most once per 128 ticks on top of
that. Painting now invalidates like erasing does.

Team::dirtyGlobalGradient also marks the local gradients dirty. They
depend on the same forbidden bits, and nothing else ever invalidated
them; on generated maps this was masked until the immobile-unit fix
made local gradients usable at all.

The harness paints two forbidden rows through OrderAlterForbidden with
one gap, checks that a unit inside the local window and one outside it
both route through the gap, closes it and checks that both are cut off
at once. It fails on the unfixed code.

commits.subject: Decode replay orders against the replay's format version (#177)
commits.body:
* Decode replay orders against the replay's format version

NetSendOrder::decodeData hardcoded VERSION_MINOR when handing the
payload to Order::getOrder. That is correct for live network traffic,
where both peers run this build, but wrong for a replay: a replay is a
stored format that may predate the running build, and ReplayReader
accepts anything from REPLAY_MINIMUM_VERSION_MINOR up.

Nothing misparses today. OrderCreate's flagRadius gate at version 78 is
the only version gate anywhere in the order layer, and it sits below the
replay floor of 86, so every order in every accepted replay decodes
identically at 86, 87 and 88. The next order-format gate would not be so
lucky -- it would silently misread every replay written before it, with
no error and no checksum to catch it.

Carry the version on NetSendOrder instead of changing the decodeData
signature, which is a NetMessage virtual with 62 overrides. It defaults
to VERSION_MINOR, so the network path and the writer are unaffected;
only ReplayReader overrides it, from the version in the replay's own
header.

ReplayStepCounterTest gains a case asserting the version actually
reaches Order::getOrder. Since no order parses differently across the
supported replay range, the plumbing has to be observed directly rather
than inferred from a decoded order; the test's stubbed getOrder records
the version it was called with. Verified to fail before this change.

G2 replay verification is byte-equal against the cpp-refactor baseline.

* Strengthen replay version tests and simplify comments

commits.subject: Refresh a resource-fetch target when its gradient is rebuilt stale (#209)
commits.body:
* Refresh a resource-fetch target when its gradient is rebuilt stale

resourceAvailableUpdate() sets a fetching unit's targetX/Y once, by
ascending the resource gradient, when the task starts. pathfindResource()
re-reads the same gradient fresh every action instead. Map::syncStep
round-robins one rebuild per tick over every gradient in use, and neither
Map::decResource nor Resource::clear() invalidates the cached gradient
directly, so a resource depleted or replaced out from under a walking
unit leaves the stored target pointing at a tile the current gradient no
longer agrees is the goal, even though the unit has already correctly
rerouted. targetX/Y also drive the debug path line (hotkey T).

Add a cheap per-action check in handleMovementGoingToResource: if the
gradient no longer marks the stored target as its goal, re-ascend it
from the unit's current position, same call as task assignment.

New ResourceFetchTargetHarness (test/, wired as the
resource-fetch-target-test scons alias) reproduces the staleness with a
real engine and depleted resource tile, and fails without the fix. Not
wired into .github/workflows/build.yml: pushing that file needs a token
with the workflow scope this one lacks.

commits.subject: Hold the map animations still while the game is paused (#221)
commits.body:
* Hold the clouds and the smoke still while the game is paused

Reported in #76: "Pause should pause clouds and smoke, too". Pausing
stops the simulation but not these two eye-candy animations, which run
off the render loop instead.

Smoke emission was already pause-safe, gated on game.stepCounter, which
does not advance while paused. Ageing was not: drawParticles() stepped
p->age and the physics on every draw, so existing puffs kept drifting
and expired mid-pause. It now takes an `advance` flag.

Freezing the clouds needs more than a frozen time value, because the
wind offset in DynamicClouds::compute() is an accumulator that advances
by a fixed amount per call regardless of what `time` says. compute()
gains an `advanceWind` flag for that, and the shape term reads a
separate `cloudTime` clock that stops while paused. The viewport
tracking still runs, so scrolling a paused game keeps the clouds
anchored to the map rather than sliding with the screen.

The water is left alone: it is driven by the existing `time` counter,
and #76 asked only for clouds and smoke.

Render-only; no order, save or network state is touched.

Opus 5 helped authoring this commit.

* Add the drawMap definition the pause flag was declared for

The previous commit added `animationsPaused` to Game::drawMap's
declaration and its two call sites but left the definition behind, so
the tree did not build.

Opus 5 helped authoring this commit.

* Freeze the water along with the clouds and the smoke

Reviewer call: a paused world with shimmering water is only half
frozen. `time` drove nothing but drawMapWater, so the separate cloud
clock existed solely to keep the water running; both collapse back into
one counter that stops while paused.

DynamicClouds::compute still needs its `advanceWind` flag: the wind
offset accumulates per call, not per time tick, so a frozen `time`
alone would leave the clouds drifting.

commits.subject: Anchor an entering unit's sprite on its own tile, not its map slot (#231)
commits.body:
* Anchor an entering unit's sprite on its own tile, not its map slot

PR #218 changed Game::drawUnit to derive the sprite origin from the tile the
draw loop found the unit on (`px = x * 32`) instead of converting
unit->posX/posY, so that a unit sitting on a map seam keeps the copy at
the opposite screen edge instead of collapsing to one occurrence.

Those two tiles agree for every action that clears the old map slot and
claims the destination one. Entering a building is the deliberate
exception: Unit::handleActionEnteringBuilding leaves the map slot on the
tile the unit is leaving so the unit stays drawable, while posX/posY
already name the building tile. Game::integrity() enforces exactly this
(test/EnteringUnitSaveHarness.cpp: "entering unit registered at
destination is invalid"). Anchoring on the stale slot ran the arrival
interpolation `px -= dx*(255-delta)>>3` one square early, so a glob
snapped back a square and walked into the tile it came from.

Keep the per-occurrence anchor and recover the unit's own tile from it by
folding in the signed wrapped offset to posX/posY — the same
anchor-recovery idiom PR #218 uses for building footprints in
drawMapGroundBuildings, but signed, because a unit's slot can sit one
square behind its position as well as ahead of it.

The arithmetic lives in src/render/UnitDrawGeometry.h so it can be tested
without a GraphicContext; UnitDrawGeometryTest covers the coinciding
case, all eight entry directions, and the seam occurrences on their own
and combined with an entry across the seam.

Fixes #230.

Opus 5 helped authoring this commit.

* Render the enter-the-building step and compare it against the same walk

UnitDrawGeometryTest pins the arithmetic, but nothing checked that the real
render path puts the glob where the arithmetic says. This adds a GL harness
that draws the state issue #230 is about and compares framebuffers.

A unit on its final step into a building keeps its map slot on the tile it is
leaving while posX/posY already name the building tile, so the draw loop visits
it one square behind itself. Nothing in Game::drawUnit reads displacement, so at
equal delta that state must render pixel-for-pixel like the same step expressed
as an ordinary walk onto the destination tile. The harness renders both over
five points of one step and reports any difference in pixels against the 32 px
tile size.

Against the pre-fix anchor it reports exactly -32 px at delta 0 — one tile
backwards, which is the reported symptom. With the fix all five deltas match.

The comparison uses the unit-only render, which has no animated water or clouds
to make two frames differ by themselves; a second pass captures terrain, glob
and inn together as scene-delta<N>.png purely so the animation can be looked at
by eye.

CI already installs xvfb and mesa for the fullscreen aspect harness, so wiring
this in is a two-liner; test/README.md carries the step verbatim. It is not
applied here because the push token has no workflow scope.

commits.subject: Walk the hiring buckets by building, not by index (#225)
commits.body:
* Walk the hiring buckets by building, not by index

Team::updateAllBuildingTasks walks buildingsNeedingUnits[priority] by
index and keeps a parallel foundPer vector, sized once, saying which
buildings hired last round and should be asked again. Every subscribe*
call ends in updateCallLists, which re-registers the building and can drop
it from the bucket, so the vector is reordered and resized under the loop
and foundPer[j] stops describing the building now at j. Buildings get
skipped for the rest of the tick, or asked again after they already gave
up.

Instrumenting a full AI game counted 6716 resizes and 648 reorders in one
game on this code.

Take a copy of the bucket and carry the flag with the building: the
buildings that hired form the next round, and nothing that happens to the
bucket meanwhile can misattribute a flag. A building that joins the bucket
mid-tick now waits for the next tick rather than being picked up part way
through the pass.

The simulation changed, so VERSION_MINOR and the replay floor move to 92.

commits.subject: Let units survive building destruction (#185) (#186)
commits.body:
Units inside a building used to die with it. Building::kill() now puts
them back on the map alive, on a free tile of the footprint first and
then the ring around it (Building::findExpelTile), so a building
surrounded by enemies still spawns its occupants on its own tiles; a
unit with no free tile at all still dies. A unit halfway through the
door steps back onto the tile it came from.

Expelled units keep the share of the meal or healing they already sat
through; training stays all-or-nothing. A started meal still costs the
inn one wheat, so nobody eats for free (Unit::applyPartialInsideBenefit,
Unit::expelFromBuilding). Capacity does not change with damage: a
building holds its full type->maxUnitInside until it dies.

Game::checkBuildingsDoNotOverlapAndHealMissing skips dead buildings:
kill() clears the footprint and stamping it back left a dangling id.

test/BuildingExpelHarness.cpp links the real engine and covers the
destroyed inn, the no-free-tile case and pro-rata healing, each
followed by real simulation steps and an integrity check. Like
TrappedUnitLifecycleTest it touches one resource gradient at setup,
since the round-robin in Map::syncStep skips fields that were never
allocated. CI builds and runs it under a timeout.

commits.subject: Apportion fetch jobs, and price a loaded candidate instead of refusing it (#223)
commits.body:
* Apportion fetch jobs across the resources a building wants

A building scored each candidate resource by neededResource(), which is
derived from resources[] alone and does not fall when a unit subscribes to
fetch one. Team::updateAllBuildingTasks hires in a loop that calls
subscribeToBringResourcesStep() repeatedly within a single tick, so every
pass re-read the same unchanged number and the score, distance / need, kept
naming whichever resource was nearest. A market site next to trees hired
eight wood fetchers for its four wood and none at all for its four stone;
the surplus carriers then arrived at a full site, could not deposit, and
were re-hired for the stone still holding the wood, which the next harvest
overwrote.

Choose the resource by apportionment instead of per unit. Sainte-Lague
priority, target / (2 * served + 1), picks the resource whose served share
sits furthest below its target share, counting subscribed units alongside
deliveries that landed, and distance then chooses which unit fills that
job. Targets of 4 and 4 interleave; targets of 4 and 1 give wood, wood,
algue, wood, wood. A unit already carrying something the building wants
still delivers ahead of the apportionment, because it costs no fetch trip
at all, and that path is subscription-aware in its own right.

considerUnitForResources split into considerUnitForBuilding, the part that
does not depend on a resource, and considerUnitForResource, which scores
one. The candidate scan runs per resource, so its rejection tallies reset
per scan and the info panel cannot count one unit once per resource.

FetchApportionmentTest covers the ranking, including that hiring stops
exactly at the targets. FetchApportionmentHarness reproduces the market
site in a real engine and asserts 4 wood and 4 stone; it reports 8 and 0
without this change.

The simulation changed, so VERSION_MINOR and the replay floor move to 91.

Opus 5 helped authoring this commit.

* Price a loaded fetch candidate instead of refusing it

Hiring consulted empty-handed candidates as a tier, and only looked at
units carrying something the building cannot take when that tier came up
empty. So a loaded unit standing at the door lost to an empty one anywhere
on the map, however far away, and the job went to the longer trip.

Score them together and charge the loaded unit a fixed detour instead. Five
tiles is enough that an empty-handed unit a short walk further away still
wins, which leaves the cargo with its carrier long enough for a building
that does want it to hire the unit first, and small enough that a unit far
enough ahead is still the better hire.

Merging the two passes also reaches a unit carrying a resource this
building wants but has already fully subscribed. Neither pass took it
before: the delivery pass had no room for another of that resource, and the
fetch-out pass only looked at units carrying something unneeded.

FetchApportionmentHarness gains two cases. Two candidates placed
symmetrically about the site score the same and the empty-handed one is
hired whichever of them holds the cargo, so neither position nor scan order
decides it. A loaded candidate six tiles ahead is hired despite the
penalty; without this change the empty one at eighteen takes the job.

Opus 5 helped authoring this commit.

commits.subject: Discuss contribution, review, and coding-agent policies (#173)
commits.body:
* Propose collaboration and coding-agent policies for discussion

* Welcome substantive engine and gameplay proposals in draft policy

* Keep agent guide focused on repository navigation and shared rules

* Require cross-platform simulation checksum verification

* Allow author self-merge for validated low-risk changes; fix doc drift

Review and merge ownership: the author may merge their own change
directly once it is low-risk or backed by strong validation evidence,
with all feedback addressed or none raised. Substantive engine/
gameplay changes and policy changes still need an independent human
maintainer regardless of validation quality. Require validation claims
to be backed by checkable artifacts (saves, replays, checksums,
screenshots/video, performance tables), not prose assertions.

Split save-state backward compatibility into its own reminder,
distinct from the more readily reset replay/network compatibility
question, and add a short "Preserving feel" note: engine-correct
changes can still change pacing, art style or difficulty, and that
needs a maintainer actually playing the result.

Fix a Markdown table in AGENTS.md broken by a stray blank line, and
restore the chamfer-cap note in docs/development-notes.md, which had
been garbled into an unrelated sentence about parallelizing gradients
and lost its file pointer and Borgefors context in the process.

Add a handful of short technical reminders mined from recent review
feedback: speculative scoring must be genuinely read-only, simulation
work must never be bounded by wall-clock time, new regression harnesses
must be wired into CI, bug fixes need a negative control, and retained
caches need an explicit bound.

commits.body: Merging directly. CI green on all three platforms, no merge conflicts, no reviewer objections. Stacked map-generator work (#240) follows.

commits.subject: Stop Map::syncStep from spinning when no gradient is allocated (#243)
commits.body:
The per-step round robin looped `while (!updated)` and only ever left
through the returns inside its scans. Since gradients are allocated
lazily (cac37e99), a team set without a single allocated field never
reaches a return: a fresh world, a game with no teams, or a loaded game
before any unit asks for a field hangs the whole game step.

Two passes are enough: the first finds the next field still due, the
second runs on freshly reset flags and finds the first allocated field.
Finding nothing on the second pass means nothing is allocated.

Drop the getResourceGradient workarounds the expulsion and trapped-unit
harnesses needed to get past the loop, and step a bare world in the
expulsion harness so the hang would fail the test instead of the CI
timeout.

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

commits.subject: Round-trip gradients: send workers to the resource nearest for the whole trip (#244)
commits.body:
* Send workers to the resource that is nearest for the round trip

A worker fetching for a building walked to the resource nearest to
itself, which is often on the far side of the base from the building it
delivers to. Buildings now own a round-trip gradient per resource type
and swim class: every tile of that resource is seeded with the cost of
carrying from beside it to the building, so descending the gradient
minimises the trip to the resource plus the trip back. Hiring and the
choice of the next resource after a delivery score by the same distance,
and a unit heading for a resource for a building follows it, falling
back to the plain resource gradient when blocked or stale.

Map::propagateGradient accepts seeds at any cost for this; seeds beyond
its bucket window enter the sweep when it reaches their cost.

Round-trip gradients are built on demand, refreshed at most every 40
ticks and freed after 500 ticks without use.

(cherry picked from commit 02185c5d100b44dc4cad6c099ae6af78b1ca4c85)

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

* Free a building's idle round-trip gradients on a timer

They were only dropped when the same building rebuilt one of its
gradients, so a building that stopped fetching kept every field it had
ever built. On a 512x512 map with 1400 units that reached 820 MB. Each
building now sweeps its unused fields every 256 ticks.

(cherry picked from commit 53627aef6d7cccb1ebcefcaa66eb16c7e8f59f6e)

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

* Free a building's gradients unused for 500 ticks, not only its round-trip ones

Every building that ever hired kept its full-map gradient per swim class
for good, although at any moment only the buildings with fetchers need
one. In a two-hour game on a 512x512 map with 250 buildings alive that
was most of 895 MB. The sweep that already drops idle round-trip fields
now drops idle building gradients too; the next unit that asks rebuilds.

(cherry picked from commit 687b0c60734859df9d362318ed7adf0ed78c7f82)

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

* Estimate the carry leg when a building has no round-trip field yet

The scorer's two arms were on different scales. With a field, roundTrip
is a real round trip; without one the fallback was distBuilding +
distResource, the walk out plus however far the unit happens to be from
the building, which for a unit standing at the building is half a round
trip. Which arm a resource gets turns on whether anything has fetched it
for this building yet, so a resource already being fetched was ranked
against a fresh one on two scales. Estimate the carry leg instead: a
unit at the building carries about as far as it walks out, and a unit
at the resource carries about the building distance, so distResource +
max(distBuilding, distResource) is exact at both ends and no worse than
the old sum in between. No field is built for this; the numbers are
already in hand.

RoundTripHungerGateHarness covers the hunger gate (the walk to the
resource, not the whole trip, decides whether a unit is hireable) and
the fallback score; the second case fails without this fix, reporting
a one-way 14 instead of the round trip of 24.

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

* Save the round-trip fields with the map runtime state

Since the continuation state (format 91) a saved game carries every
cached routing field and its timestamps, so a loaded game continues bit
for bit. The round-trip fields, their refresh and last-use stamps and
the building gradient's last-use stamp were not saved, so after a load
hiring scored by the estimate where the uninterrupted game read a field,
and the two games drifted apart within twenty steps
(SavegameSafetyHarness, continuation check).

They join the building part of the map runtime section under format 95.
Older saves load as before with the fields empty. The replay floor moves
to 95 as well: routing and hiring by round trip change the simulation.

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

commits.subject: Swap fetching jobs between units when both trips get shorter (#197)
commits.body:
* Follow the round-trip gradient for the resource-fetch target too

targetX/Y for a fetch task (also the debug path line, hotkey T) are set
once, by ascending the plain resource gradient, when the task starts.
pathfindResource() re-reads whichever gradient actually governs the
per-tick step -- the round-trip field when attachedBuilding has one and
it is valid here, the plain resource gradient otherwise -- and either
field can be rebuilt, or the preference between them can flip, while
the unit is still walking. The stored target never tracked either
change, so the debug line and the range checks that read targetX/Y
could point at the nearest tile to the unit while the unit actually
walked toward the cheaper round trip through a farther one.

Add Map::isGradientPeak: whether a tile is a local maximum of a
gradient, true for anywhere getGlobalGradientDestination's ascent could
end, including a round-trip field whose seeded goal is a finite cost
rather than the type's max the way GRADIENT_AT_GOAL is (so its own
'reached exact goal' check does not generalize). handleMovementGoingToResource
now resolves the same gradient pathfindResource prefers and re-ascends
from the unit's position whenever the stored target stops being a peak
of it -- a cheap check every action, the ascent itself only when stale.

New ResourceFetchTargetHarness (test/, wired as the
resource-fetch-target-test scons alias) seeds a tile close to the unit
but far from the building and one far from the unit but close to it,
confirms the target follows the cheaper round trip rather than the
nearer tile, and that it refreshes once that tile is harvested away.
Fails without the fix. Full test/TestsRunner suite (169 tests) passes;
scons release=1 and release=1 server=1 build clean.

(cherry picked from commit 6bb00b01a8d8cc55eaf02c04942691adc6b3413a)

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

* Swap fetching jobs between units when both trips get shorter

A unit that becomes free takes the job of whichever building asks first,
however far away, and units never trade jobs. Team::swapTask compares a
fetcher's job with every team mate's: a job costs the round trip for an
empty-handed unit or the delivery distance for one carrying that
resource, and when the two trips together shrink by more than four tiles
the units exchange building, resource and target and keep walking from
where they are. It runs for a unit right after it is hired and, four
units a tick, over every fetcher every 256 ticks.

(cherry picked from commit 4ba5c919f3aee53dc1399cce49d9653885f96943)

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

* Swap jobs across swim classes when the gradients already exist

Requiring the same swim class was only a proxy for what matters: that
every cost in the comparison is read from a gradient some unit already
keeps alive, so a comparison never builds one. Check that directly, so
a swimmer and a walker swap whenever both fields are there.

(cherry picked from commit 3613f934a47a5cacfad9c6484a358008e984def1)

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

* Swap inns between hungry units when both walks get shorter

A hungry unit books the nearest inn with a free meal, and the booking
takes the meal: the next unit, standing closer to that inn, finds it
full and walks to the next one, crossing the first on the way. Two
units heading for the wrong inns each is the food side of the crossing
that swapTask fixes for fetching.

Team::swapInn runs the moment a unit books its place. It compares the
unit's walk with every team mate still walking to an inn of this team,
reading only the building gradients that choosing an inn already built
(or the crow-flight distance for a flyer), and when trading inns
shortens the two walks together by more than four tiles it moves both
bookings: guest lists, attached and target building. Each inn keeps its
head count, so the meals stay reserved. A trade that would put an inn
beyond what a unit can still walk is not made.

Inn bookings are rare next to hiring, so one scan per booking is cheap.
InnSwapHarness covers the crossing and a booking that is already the
shorter one, and walks both units into their inns afterwards.

Fable 5.1 helped authoring this commit.

commits.subject: Save the Echo AI's building-order id (#253)
commits.body:
AIEcho::Construction::BuildingOrder::id is assigned at runtime by
Echo::add_building_order via BuildingRegister::register_building and is the key
the order is known by in BuildingRegister::pending_buildings, but save() and
load() never moved it and the member had no initialiser. Every pending building
order restored from a savegame therefore carried an uninitialised heap value,
which Echo::update_building_orders then used as a map key for issue_order() and
passed to AssignWorkers. Consequences: a game resumed from a save with AI
players was not reproducible run to run, and a resumed multiplayer game could
desync without packet loss or a version mismatch.

Serialise id, gated on versionMinor >= 96, and default the member to -1. Saves
written before 96 do not carry the field, so Echo::load hands those orders a
fresh br.register_building() key rather than a sentinel; the BuildingRegister is
loaded earlier in the same function, with its building_id counter restored from
the stream, so the new key is valid and cannot collide with a restored entry.

VERSION_MINOR 95 -> 96 and REPLAY_MINIMUM_VERSION_MINOR -> 96. The replay floor
has to move because a replay header is a full serialised game state, so starting
a replay is a load and goes through the same path. MINIMUM_VERSION_MINOR stays
58: existing saves still load.

Adds test/EchoBuildingOrderSaveLoadTest.cpp covering the version-96 round trip,
an unregistered order's -1 surviving the Uint32 on the wire, and a pre-96 stream
leaving the -1 sentinel with every following field still decoding from the right
offset. Negative control: removing the two serialisation lines fails exactly the
"id preserved" assertion and leaves the other eleven passing.

commits.subject: Shrink the audio device buffer and skip opening it while muted (#252)
commits.body:
SoundMixer asked SDL for a 16384-frame buffer (371 ms at 44100 Hz), and
SDL_CloseAudio has to wait for the in-flight callback before the process can
exit. Muting did not help: the constructor zeroed the volumes and opened the
device anyway, so a silent session still ran the audio thread, still decoded
Ogg, and still paid the full exit wait.

The fade length and the device buffer size were the same constant by accident:
the ramp table was indexed by position within one callback, so one buffer was
exactly one fade. They are now separate concepts -- FADE_SAMPLE_COUNT and
DEVICE_FRAME_COUNT -- with a new fadePos member carrying the ramp across
callbacks, so a fade lasts the same wall-clock time at any buffer size. With
that in place the device buffer drops to 1024 frames, and a muted start leaves
the device closed until setVolume() opens it on unmute.

Follow-up fixes in this PR:

- While the device is closed nothing is playing, so setNextTrack moves both
  actTrack and nextTrack. Previously actTrack stayed pinned to the first track
  ever selected, and unmuting resumed that one: the intro replayed and then
  looped (menu.ogg never played), and unmuting mid-game played menu music over
  the match.
- A fade now spans sixteen callbacks, so a track change can arrive mid-fade --
  GameMusicController can emit on consecutive 40 ms ticks. Restarting the fade
  cut the incoming track off mid-mix; the request is now queued in pendingTrack
  and started when the running fade lands.

Verification: music output is bit-identical to master for the first 3 seconds
(max |diff| = 0 over 132300 frames). New test/SoundMixerTrackSelectionHarness
drives mixaudio() against the real ogg tracks and covers both follow-up fixes;
it was confirmed to fail on the unfixed tree one bug at a time. TestsRunner 187
tests OK. CI green on ubuntu 22.04/24.04 and mingw-w64.

Measured on real hardware (Realtek ALC1220), which the original dummy-driver
numbers understated by roughly an order of magnitude:

  SDL_CloseAudio   pulseaudio 783 -> 49 ms,  raw ALSA 1741 -> 113 ms
  full game exit   sound on  911 -> 173 ms,  muted    886 -> 114 ms

Callback rate at 1024 frames is exactly on target on both drivers with no
underrun warnings. Windows audio remains untested by anyone; mingw builds but
never opens a device.

Not addressed here: GameGUI::~GameGUI saves the whole settings struct when
rememberUnit is set, so a command-line override such as -m becomes permanently
persisted after one game.

commits.subject: Re-roll the harness's river map instead of asserting the first try (#262)
commits.body:
CustomGameSetupHarness aborted on assert(generator.generateMap(g, d)) often
enough to be a real nuisance: 1 failure in 25 runs on an untouched tree, which
across two Linux images is roughly a 1 in 12 chance of a spurious red on any PR.
It went red on #252 that way, on a change touching only the sound mixer.

The generator is not at fault. A river roll that cannot seat four starting
colonies is a normal outcome: Map::makeRandomMap gives up when no grass patch is
left far enough from the teams already placed, and Game::makeRandomMap gives up
when the swarm or its workers will not fit. Both the game
(CustomGameScreen::generateMap) and the eight-landscape loop directly above this
call already re-roll up to five times rather than treat a failed roll as an
error. This one call did neither, and now does.

Re-rolling rather than pinning a seed is deliberate: the terrain comes from
HeightMap, which draws on rand() rather than syncRand, so a seed would not
reproduce the same map across platforms -- and a seed that happens to seat four
colonies under glibc could fail every time under mingw or macOS libc.

Verification: 200 consecutive runs of the fixed harness, 200 passes 0 failures,
against 24/25 for the same tree without the change. At the measured per-roll rate
200 clean runs would happen by chance with probability ~3e-4. Test-only change.

commits.subject: Scale the whole interface with the desktop's scale factor (#250)
commits.body:
Every glob2 screen is laid out in fixed pixels against a roughly 640x480 design:
fonts load at 20/13/10 px, the sidebar is 160 px, the top stat bar is a literal
16 px, and nothing reads the desktop's scale. On a 5120x2816 display at 175% the
stat-bar digits are half the cap height of the desktop text beside them.

Rather than multiply ~950 layout literals across 33 screens, this reuses the
logical-resolution path setRes() already has for fullscreen letterboxing: the
window keeps its size, the interface is laid out on a surface of window/uiScale,
and nextFrame() / the GL viewport scale it back up. windowToLogical() already
maps input back, so hit-testing is unchanged, and every screen grows by one
factor so the proportions between them are preserved.

The factor comes from GLOB2_UI_SCALE, then the new Settings -> Display ->
Interface scale preference, then the desktop. SDL_GetDisplayDPI reports the
panel's physical DPI rather than the fraction the user chose, so the desktop
value is read from Xft.dpi in the X resource database -- what GTK, Qt and
Xwayland read. libX11 is dlopened, so no new build dependency and non-X11 builds
simply report no scale.

Also in this PR: the 640x480 layout floor now holds against the scale on a live
window resize. setRes() clamped uiScale but updateWindowSize() did not, and both
SDL_SetWindowMinimumSize calls passed the unscaled minimum, so a resizable window
(the default) dragged to 640x480 at scale 1.75 laid the interface out on 366x274
-- narrower than the 368px main menu panel. The minimum is a floor on the logical
surface, so the window's own minimum is now the scaled one. WindowResizeHarness
covers it; it previously could not, because its context is built at 640x480 where
the scale is reduced to 1 and nothing is stretched.

Verification: stat bar 16 -> 28 px, exactly 1.75x; main menu panel 368 -> 644 px;
auto-detection with Xft.dpi 168 produces the same 644 px panel as asking for 175%
explicitly. TestsRunner 187 OK, WindowResizeHarness passes software and GL, the
campaign harnesses and translation checks pass. No simulation code reads the
screen settings, so replays and lockstep are unaffected.

Known limits, accepted: text is scaled with the frame and so is softer than a
native render -- crisp text needs higher-resolution assets and font loading at
scale, deliberately a separate change. A maintainer reviewed the before/after
renders and judged it legible. Auto-detection covers X11 and Xwayland only; the
desktop scale is read once at startup. The three new strings are machine-
translated in all 33 languages.

commits.subject: Fix middle-button panning being dropped, and hold the automatic torus while panning (#249)
commits.body:
* Apply pending mouse motion before the button event that ends it

GameGUI::step coalesces mouse motion and replays only the last event
after the poll loop, so within one frame every button event is handled
before any movement. Middle-button panning lives entirely in the motion
handler and a middle-button release clears panPushed, so a pan whose
drag and release landed in the same frame was discarded outright: the
deferred motion ran with panPushed already false and the viewport never
moved. A flick that fits inside one frame lost all of its travel, which
is why panning felt like it randomly needed a second click. The left
button was shielded by the existing do-not-skip-map-cells flush, which
is gated on SDL_BUTTON(1).

Flush the pending motion before handling a button event instead. Traced
under Xvfb: a 100 px down-move-up flick inside one frame moved the
camera 0 px before, 100 px after, and a slow multi-frame drag still
moves exactly 100 px with no double application.

Opus 5 helped authoring this commit.

* Always start a pan on middle-click, including over the right panel

Middle-clicking the right panel started a pan, except when a building
was selected: that case fell into a debug branch whose body has been
commented out for years, so the click did nothing at all and the next
one panned. Drop the dead branch and pan unconditionally.

panViewX and panViewY went write-only when panning moved to the camera
origin; remove them with it.

Opus 5 helped authoring this commit.

* Keep the automatic torus out while the middle button is held

The overview is driven by notifyMove, which only fires when the viewport
crosses a tile boundary, and it retracts 250 ms after the last such move.
Holding the middle button still mid-pan therefore looked identical to
having finished panning: the ring dropped back to the flat map under the
user's hand and unfolded again the moment they nudged the mouse.

Track the held pan alongside the existing pointerHeld gesture flag and
suspend the retract timer while it is set, so the overview stays out for
as long as the button is down and returns on release as before. GameGUI
pushes the flag once per frame instead of at press and release, since
several paths clear panPushed and the two must not drift apart.

Opus 5 helped authoring this commit.

* Review artifacts: automatic torus with the middle button held (dropped at tip)

Opus 5 helped authoring this commit.

* Drop review artifacts from the branch tip

Opus 5 helped authoring this commit.

commits.subject: Mark the units a selected building could not hire (#259)
commits.body:
The building panel already told the player how many units a selected building
could not hire and why, but not which ones, so the counts were not actionable.
While the local player has a building selected, it now remembers the units
behind each tally by gid and the map view draws a badge -- a mini "no entry"
sign -- over exactly those units.

Every reason wears the same badge rather than a shape per reason: several
reasons can apply to one unit at once with only the first recorded, so distinct
shapes would have been a promise the engine cannot keep. Which reason applies is
spelled out as text beside the badge in the panel. The badge is computed from
the circle equation rather than loaded as a sprite, so it stays exact at the
scaled-up interface sizes (#250), and carries a white border so it survives on a
red team's own units -- the units it is only ever drawn on.

Display only, and deliberately so. The tally is incremented unconditionally and
only the gid is recorded, gated on the local selection, so a client with the
building selected runs the same simulation as one without. The new members are
absent from Building::checkSum, are not serialized, and Building is never
memset, which is what makes std::vector members safe here. No version bump.

The panel rows and the map badges ask one shared gate, shouldShowFailingUnitMarkers,
so a unit can never wear a badge the panel has no row to explain, and a building
that has stopped asking for units shows neither.

Verification: failing-unit-markers harness (new, in CI under xvfb) covers
recording on and off, the rendered markers, and the deselect path;
BuildingFailureDisplayTest covers the gate. Reviewed on screen at real map size
over grass, sand, water and a red team unit.

Known follow-ups, all display-only: the most common reason ("too far from
building") frequently marks units outside the current view -- in one of six real
obstructions sampled from a 13000-tick four-AI game, selecting the building
changed zero pixels; drawUnit does a linear search of the gid lists per unit per
frame; recycled gids can briefly badge the wrong unit; and because tallies are
saved while gid lists are not, the panel can show a row with no badges until the
first hiring pass after a load.

commits.subject: Let a cached route field notice the ground moved, wherever it moved (#232)
commits.body:
A building's cached route field recorded which cells were obstacles when it was
computed, and nothing reliably told it when that stopped being true.
Game::addBuilding -- the one path every placement takes: player orders, queued
build projects, map generators, the editor, story scripts -- stamped the
footprint onto the map and told nobody. A field built while the ground was open
kept routing through it, units were hired for a building they could no longer
reach, and they only gave up once one of them was stuck long enough to force a
rebuild, at which point `locked` was set and the whole crew dropped the job at
once. Removal was never the problem: ORDER_DELETE already dirtied the rectangle
and freed every field of the team.

An earlier attempt dirtied buildings within a widened footprint. Review killed
it for three reasons, all structural: route fields span the map, so distance is
not the question -- a building sixty tiles away routes through the changed cell
just the same; the same walk read the building tile grid, which virtual
buildings are never written into, so no flag's field was reachable by it; and
ordinary demolition dirtied only the owner's buildings.

Map::topologyGeneration is bumped instead when a footprint is stamped or lifted
and when a forbidden area actually changes. Each cached field records the value
it was built at and Map::buildingGradient compares the two. Invalidation is
O(1), reads no tiles, and covers distance, flags, other teams and any future way
of moving a footprint by construction.

Deliberately not covered: resources growing or being cleared, and units becoming
immobile. Counted over one 8-player match: building=552 forbidden=458
resource=10152 immobile=50594 -- a glob stepping into a building is 82% of them.
Bumping on everything costs 47% of simulation time; the structural changes alone
cost 18%, which is 0.599 ms/tick becoming 0.706 against a 40 ms budget. Neither
exclusion can walk a unit into a wall, because Map::directionByGradient rechecks
live passability on every candidate step.

The rebuild throttle moves from 25 ticks to 100, which is what bounds the
resulting rebuild load. Measured on gd-bigarena-long (Oazis, 11 teams), 8000
ticks, master vs this branch; "stuck" counts rebuilds forced by a unit that
could not make progress -- the symptom this branch exists to remove:

    throttle    rebuilds  generation-caused  stuck   bfs time     wall
    master          2906                  0    195     2.091s   16.73s
    25 ticks       12603               9755      1     9.183s  +42.6%

commits.subject: Stop autosave from stalling the game at high speed (#260)
commits.body:
* Stop autosave from stalling the game at high speed

At 8x-40x the game froze for a fraction of a second every second or two.
Every 256 ticks GameGUI::syncStep wrote the whole game, including every
cached pathfinding gradient, to Auto_save.game. Late-game saves are
65-120 MB, and at 8x 256 ticks is about 1.3 seconds.

- Write gradient fields as one run of bytes through
  OutputStream::writeUint16Sections. The bytes and SHA1 are the same as
  per-value writes, without a virtual call, name string and SHA1 update
  per value.
- Give the atomic autosave writer a 1 MiB buffer instead of 16 KiB.
- Skip the whole-file SHA1 for autosaves; the header keeps zeros.
  Engine::haveMap, the hash's only reader, now fetches the host's copy
  of any file without a hash instead of trusting a local file.
- Scale the autosave interval with the game-speed preset so saves stay
  about 10 seconds of real time apart. Normal speed keeps ticks 79,
  335, and so on. Counting from the last save also stops a soft-paused
  game on a save tick from autosaving every frame.

Simulation checksums and replays are unchanged. At normal speed the
autosave differs from master's only in its 20 SHA1 bytes.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01LPPkz7Vd7QLMsbQfqy3kHU

* Write autosaves on a background thread and add an autosave setting

Autosave serialized the game and wrote it to disk on the game thread. At
late-game sizes (65-160 MB) the write alone took 30-70 ms, with spikes
past 180 ms, on every autosave.

- Serialize between ticks into memory, then hand the bytes to a new
  GAGCore::BackgroundFileWriter, which replaces the file through
  FileManager::writeAtomically on a worker thread. A snapshot that has
  not started writing is replaced by a newer one. The worker exists only
  while there is something to write, so waiting leaves no thread behind
  and a forked process never inherits one.
- MemoryStreamBackend appends past its end instead of resizing, which
  zero-filled every byte before writing it, and gains reserve() and
  takeContents() so the snapshot moves to the writer without a copy.
- Wait for a pending autosave before a session ends, before an in-game
  save, and when GameGUI is destroyed.
- Add Settings > Gameplay > Autosave (autosaveGames, on by default),
  translated for every language.
- Autosave now hands writeAtomically one complete buffer, which bypasses
  the stream buffer, so the 1 MiB atomic-write buffer from the previous
  commit no longer has any effect; revert it.

Saved bytes, simulation checksums and replays are unchanged.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01LPPkz7Vd7QLMsbQfqy3kHU

* Hash autosaves on the writer thread, and compare map SHA1s the right way round

Autosaves had dropped their whole-file SHA1 to keep hashing off the game
thread, which made a client joining from an autosave always download it.
Game::save now records what the hash needs in a DeferredGameSHA1 and the
BackgroundFileWriter applies it on its worker, so autosave bytes match an
inline-hashed save again and Engine::haveMap is back to master's logic.

MapHeader::operator== has compared the SHA1 inverted since 8cf81c9d3, so
haveMap re-downloaded identical files and trusted different ones. Fixed,
with a harness check that fails on the old comparison.

commits.subject: Draw the torus view's map markers at the atlas's scale, not the window's (#275)
commits.body:
* Draw the torus view's map markers at the atlas's scale, not the window's

At a 300% interface scale the torus view's status bars turn into grey blobs, the
selected building's ring becomes a thick band, and the white circles on the units
working for it are gone entirely.

GL rasterises lines at a width in the pixels of whatever is being drawn into, so
setScaledLineWidth() multiplies by drawableScale(), the factor the window stretches
the logical surface by. That is right for the window and wrong for the torus, which
renders the whole map into an offscreen atlas at one texel per world pixel: outlines
land there three times too thick. The bars show it plainly, because drawPointBar()
paints its filled segments as quads, which stay correct, and its empty ones as
drawRect() outlines, which at a 3 px stroke fill the 4x4 cell solid. Track the
current target instead: rasterScale() reports the offscreen target's pixels per
logical pixel while one is set and the window's otherwise, and the atlas pass sets
it to the atlas's texels per world pixel.

Separately, drawOverlayInfos() skips its whole selection block while the torus is
active, and drawTorusMap() mirrored only the selected building's own circle. The
white circles marking the units working for it, and the circle on a selected
resource, were never drawn at all, and the building circle was always blue instead
of blue, orange or red by ownership. Draw them onto the atlas, anchored to the map
surface, the way the flat view draws them over it.

Validation: 190 local unit tests; torus-render-test in GL at interface scale 1 and 3
and in software; point-bar-render-test in GL and software; the fullscreen aspect and
window resize harnesses. The new atlas assertions in TorusRenderIntegrationTest both
fail on the unfixed code. CI gains a torus-render-test run at GLOB2_UI_SCALE=3, which
is what makes the line-width assertion bite. Before/after screenshots from a seeded
-test-games run at 2560x1440 and 300% are in the pull request.

commits.subject: Rasterise interface text for the screen it is drawn on (#263)
commits.body:
* Rasterise interface text at the size it is drawn on a scaled screen

Whenever the frame is not presented one logical pixel per screen pixel, the GL
viewport resamples it, but glyphs are rasterised once at the authored font size,
so text is the only part of the interface that cannot use the pixels it is given.
This happens at every interface scale above 100 %, and also at 100 % when the
display cannot deliver the requested resolution exactly: a fullscreen 3456x2234
on a 16-inch MacBook is presented at 3456x2168, which reduces every glyph by 3 %.

TrueTypeFont now keeps two font handles. Metrics stay on the authored size, so
getStringWidth and getStringHeight report exactly what they reported before and
no widget moves. Rasterisation uses a second handle opened at size * scale,
reopened, and the string cache dropped, when the scale changes. The scale is the
new GraphicContext::textRenderScale(): drawable pixels per logical pixel, and 1
for the software renderer, which composes the whole frame in the logical surface
and caps every glyph there anyway.

Hinting rounds every font size differently, so the second raster is not exactly
scale times the first: "Editor" measures 61 logical pixels at size 20 but 118
device pixels at size 40, which is 59. Drawing it into the rectangle the authored
size measures would stretch it by three percent, and nearest-neighbour sampling
turns that into pixel columns repeated or dropped inside single glyphs. The
raster is therefore drawn at its own size from the same origin.

Only the screen carries that scaled viewport, so the second raster is used only
when the target is the screen. An overlay dialog composes itself on a surface of
logical pixels, and DrawableSurface has no scaled blit to resample with, so those
keep the authored raster and look exactly as before. The cache key carries which
raster an entry holds.

Reopening the window for another resolution or interface scale creates a new GL
context, which starts at the GL defaults and leaves every texture name from the
old context dangling. The cached GL state was not reset with it, so the first
draws after such a switch skipped the enables they needed and filled white
quads. GLState::resetCache() now runs with the new context, and the string cache
drops itself when the context generation changes.

test/TextRasterHarness.cpp is the regression. It requires the reported string
sizes to survive a scale change unchanged, the frame to carry detail inside the
scale-sized pixel blocks, the drawn glyphs to match a string rasterised
independently for that screen at a magnifying, a fractional and a reducing scale,
and text drawn on an overlay surface to still reach the screen. Each check fails
against the implementation it guards. CI builds and runs it under Xvfb alongside
the other presentation harnesses.

Simulation, saves, replays and the network protocol are untouched: a 600-tick
headless run of games/gd-small-2ai.game keeps checksum 6b785f48.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Name GAGCore::Font in the text raster harness, which X11's Font shadows on Linux

GraphicContextPrivate.h pulls in the GL headers, and on Linux those bring
X11/X.h with its 'typedef XID Font', so the unqualified name under
'using namespace GAGCore' is ambiguous and the harness does not compile.

commits.subject: Read one worker level where hiring read harvest and the menu read build (#256)
commits.body:
* Read one worker level where hiring read harvest and the menu read build

A worker has two schooling levels that mean the same thing. Only the
school raises either, it raises both in one visit (upgradeInParallel),
and nothing else in the game tells them apart: the harvest level gated
which building tier a worker may work for and its chop speed, the build
level gated which upgrades the menu offers (Team::maxBuildLevel) and its
fill speed. So the hiring gate and the upgrade button read different
numbers for the same question, and the map editor offered two boxes for
one value. Set apart in the editor, a unit could be allowed to upgrade a
building it was then refused by.

Make it one value:

- Unit::workerLevel() reads it; Unit::setWorkerLevel() sets both halves
  and their performance together. The hiring gate, Team::maxBuildLevel
  and the fetch ranking read through it.
- A unit loaded from a save older than the change keeps the higher of the
  two, so maps edited before this keep working and cannot desync on it.
- A non-parallel upgrade of build or harvest raises both.
- The editor keeps the build box and drops the harvest box; the unit
  panel drops the Harvest row, which always showed the Build value.

The save format and race tables are untouched; both abilities are still
stored and still drive their own speeds.

A real-engine harness (test/LevelGateHarness.cpp, target level-gate-test,
run in CI) checks the gate against completed buildings and sites and that a
level-2 site hires build 1 with harvest 0 and refuses the reverse.

Simulation behaviour can change for maps with the two levels apart, so
VERSION_MINOR goes to 98 and replays older than that are refused. The
number lives beside master's other save-format gates as
FILE_FORMAT_VERSION_ONE_WORKER_LEVEL in src/FileFormatVersions.h, and the
load-time evening-out reads it, so the next time master moves there is one
place to change and a grep that finds it.

commits.subject: Map generation improvements: modular framework and twelve new generators (#240)
commits.body:
* Modularize map generation and add new generators

* Sort map generators by quality

* Refine map generator quality order

* Make Contested Commons the first and default generator

* Fix rectangular map previews and wrapped colony start coordinates

* Keep review reports and generated screenshots out of the repository

* Bridge CustomGamePreferences through the legacy generator descriptor

#238 (already merged) added CustomGamePreferences.h, which serializes
CustomGameSetup::generator by taking Sint32 MapGenerationDescriptor::*
member pointers directly. #240 replaced generator's type with
GenerationRequest, whose method-specific options live in a generic
std::map<std::string,int> instead of fixed struct fields — an
architecture change, not a rename — so the file no longer compiled.

- CustomGamePreferences::encode()/decode() now convert through
  toLegacyDescriptor()/fromLegacyDescriptor() (the compatibility
  adapter #240 already built for exactly this kind of interop), so the
  on-disk wire format and its corruption-recovery bounds are unchanged.
  decode()'s method-validity check now asks the live GeneratorRegistry
  instead of a hardcoded 1-8 range, so it stays correct as generators
  are added or retired.
- Widened several fields() bounds (terrain weights 0-64 -> 0-100,
  riverDiameter's max 64 -> 65, oldIslandSize 1-64 -> 1-70) to match
  the modular registry's current ranges. These are approximate,
  same as before: the reused legacy fields (e.g. riverDiameter also
  stands in for lake size/channel width/bridge width) don't have one
  true bound, so this is a safe envelope, not a tight per-method one.
  Without this, decode() could reject a preferences file that a normal
  save legitimately produced (oldIslandSize's own default already
  exceeded the old 1-64 bound for any method other than Isles/Old
  Islands).
- Found and fixed a related crash bug in the compatibility adapter
  itself while tracing this: Lattice and Maze register wheat/wood/
  stone/algae controls with no entry in legacyField()'s mapping table,
  so converting either method through toLegacyDescriptor/
  fromLegacyDescriptor threw an uncaught std::invalid_argument. Added
  the four missing mappings (they match pre-existing legacy struct
  fields exactly) and changed every other option with no legacy slot
  (loopiness, home-radius, cell-size, ...) from throwing to falling
  back to its control's default value, so a newer generator's full
  option set can never crash this adapter again.
- test/CustomGameSetupHarness.cpp: preferencesModel()/preferencesScreen()
  built a GenerationRequest via the same member-pointer approach;
  updated both to build a temporary MapGenerationDescriptor and convert.
  Switched preferencesModel()'s method from Old Islands to Crater Lakes
  (one of the four modern height-map generators that still exposes a
  repeat-landscape control; Old Islands never did in the new registry,
  so it always round-tripped back to 0). The per-field assertions in
  preferencesScreen() now compare against the same achievable
  conversion rather than raw field maximums, since only the options a
  method actually registers survive a GenerationRequest round trip.

Verified: full scons -j8 release=1 server=0 client build is clean.
CustomGameSetupHarness passes in default, preferences-write and
preferences-read modes. MapGeneratorDefaultsTest and
MapGeneratorStudy --catalog also pass, unaffected by the adapter fix.
