commits.subject: Fit the map fairness score to real games (#321)
commits.body:
Replaces the hand-weighted start score with a conditional-logit model fitted to 2,942 homogeneous-AI free-for-all games on randomly drawn maps. Start fitness is linear in five measurements -- distance-decayed uncontested wheat, contested territory, building sites, rivals close by and wood stock -- softmax over a map's colonies gives win probability, and fairness is 1 minus the colony-count-normalised Gini of those probabilities. Cross-validated McFadden R2 0.0278 against 0.0019 for the old score. The lobby keeps its fairest candidate roll; no simulation, save, replay or network code changed.

Adds tools/fairness_model.py (tournament, fit, remeasure, sampling), FairnessModel.h generated from the fit, start diagnostics, --report timing and --perturb, a rebuilt and translated start-quality screen, and Lava shield revision 3 with golden rows regenerated on macOS and Linux.

commits.subject: Rebuild The Glacis, Allotments and Caravanserai (revision 2) (#325)
commits.body:
The three premade-base landscapes are redesigned around their themes and
play from an ordinary swarm and the lobby's workers:

- The Glacis: bastioned star forts (one stencil, one facing per map) with a
  moat, covered way and a bare glacis ring against the woods; kitchen
  gardens behind the courtyard; streams between forts with contested fords,
  orchards and quarries; roads to the gates.
- Allotments: villages with a green and a block of plots, among warped
  parcels of strip plots round ditches (each plot tended differently),
  commons round ponds and woodlots.
- Caravanserai: oasis towns round a lake with a field ring and palm grove,
  in a desert of dune bands, scrub, mesas and irregular oases, with walled
  caravanserais between neighbours.

Premade bases, shared/Bases, Compounds, Lots and the startingWorkers hook
are removed; wallStanding moves to Walls and quarter-turn stencil helpers
join Orbits. New controls are translated in every catalog; contracts cover
envelope, resource extremes, contained growth and deliberate damage; golden
rows regenerated on macOS and Linux.

Rotation tournaments (256x256, four colonies, 45,000 ticks) against
revision 1, per colony: Nicowar peak units 64->107 (Glacis), 118->100
(Allotments), 62->120 (Caravanserai), eliminations 33/18/67 -> 11/12/11 of
96. Numbi fixes followed (swarm on open ground, compact wheat blocks, one
facing per map); the last of these is covered by sweeps and contracts only.

The map-design skill records the lessons: starting conditions are not
concepts, contrast makes features read, AI-legible openings (Numbi's
placement and food gates), facing bias of rotated stencils, local
calibration before tournaments, and new helper scripts.

commits.body:
* Add the Karst towers map generator

River valleys among limestone pinnacles: thickets of permanent stone
towers from a Turing pattern's spots, rivers routed as the cheapest walk
between rows of homes so they bend round the towers, terraced paddies of
alternating wheat and flooded ribbons along the banks, doline lakes with
sealed fields between neighbouring homes, and sinkholes with sinking
streams. Every home is an identical gated bowl of towers with an irrigated
paddy, a rim pond and gate pools, in one of four gate designs per map.

dry fords. Translations for the new strings in every catalog.

commits.body:
* Add the Bajada map generator

A desert mountain front: swaying stone ranges cut by passes between
stone shoulders, rows of alluvial fans grown as distributary trees that
split downhill and die out in sand washes, a gravel belt along the
ranges giving way to dune sand, and playa lakes with salt-flat rims,
meadows and crossings in every basin.

Every colony gets the same home fan, designed once in its own frame and
stamped over an erased footprint: a town on the fan's dry shoulder
sealed by a ring of sand corners, a garden with the kit's wheat and a
pond beside the swarm, and the fan's streams. Three designs (Broad fan,
Long fan, Twin springs) and a mirror image are drawn per map. Homes hang
evenly from one face of each range; close homes get smaller towns.

Validation checks identical homes and their crops, designed stone,
ranges uncrossable with the passes shut, sealed towns, no crops in towns
and walking routes. Contract test, macOS golden rows, docs with review
previews, and translations reviewed in every catalog.

Built over five rounds with an independent reviewer; a 516-map control
study, 4,000 random rolls (only crowding refusals) and 16 local AI games.

commits.subject: Widen rice terraces' contour bands so wheat and water can grow (#330)
commits.body:
Default corners were narrow enough that layBeaches' erosion, the
four-corner pureness test and the sway that gives the hillside its
curves left most of every terrace as unplantable mixed sand: crop
width fell to a single tile at the median (often none), and water
rows fared the same. Widened the crop and water bands, lengthened the
sway wavelengths (which also makes the curves bigger and gentler
rather than sharper, protecting width where the hillside turns),
raised the default/max waviness accordingly, and raised the
band-width control's floor since below it the guarantee broke even
with the wider bands. Verified over dozens of seeds across the full
band-width/waviness range: crop and water width both hold >= 2 tiles
everywhere and 3+ typically.

Revision bumped 1 -> 3 and macOS arm64 golden rows regenerated;
Linux rows still need a CI refresh.

Co-authored-by: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

commits.subject: Fix The Glacis failing to generate for five-pointed forts (#331)
commits.body:
Bulk-generating 100 seeds at default parameters (Mixed bastions, 4
teams, 256x256) showed a 29% failure rate. Root cause: whenever the
random bastion draw landed on five (one of Mixed's three options),
generation failed 100% of the time, deterministically:

1. The garden-splitting axis ("back") was snapped to whichever
   curtain sat nearest the true rear (kPi), rather than kPi itself.
   For an even bastion count that curtain is always exactly at kPi
   (a no-op), but five bastions has no curtain there, so the axis
   landed 36 degrees off center and threw the two rear gardens out
   of balance (319/58/14 tiles against a 40-tile floor), failing the
   "fort is too small for its gardens" check on every roll.

2. Fixing that exposed a second, previously-masked bug: a garden's
   cistern (irrigation pond) could sit close enough to a wall vertex
   that layBeaches's one-step erosion spoiled the wall's own purity,
   failing "a wall would stand on a beach". The along/across offsets
   that place a cistern assume it's tucked behind the curtain
   directly opposite it; an odd bastion count's uneven curtain
   spacing can swing that offset close enough to a neighbouring
   curtain's wall to reach it. Added an explicit guard that reverts
   any cistern vertex within beach range of a wall tile back to
   grass.

Verified with a bulk sweep: forcing five-pointed bastions failed
50/50 before, 0/50 after; the original 100-seed default-parameter
repro went from 71/100 to 100/100. A broader sweep across team
counts 1-8 and several map sizes found no other reliability defect
(a "too many colonies" refusal for teams=7 on a 256x256 map is a
separate, pre-existing capacity limit unrelated to bastion count).

Output changes for five-pointed (and other odd-bastion) forts, so
the revision is bumped 2 -> 3 and macos-arm64 golden rows updated
via MapGeneratorGoldenTest --update; linux-x86_64 rows need the same
refresh from CI. The --sweep and full golden-row comparison both
pass clean after the fix.

commits.subject: Landscape picker: tags, filters, sort, inline size/colony controls (#333)
commits.body:
* Add tags, sort order and compatibility disabling to the landscape picker

- GeneratorDefinition gains a `tags` field ("category:value" strings);
  GeneratorTags.cpp curates them centrally for all 49 playable generators
  (terrain/feature/style/fairness) from the glob2-map-design skill's
  generator-by-generator review, and GeneratorRegistry assigns them and
  requires every non-editor-only generator to have some.
- LandscapePickerScreen: a Random/Alphabetical sort segment and one filter
  dropdown per tag category, catalog-browsing style (AND across categories).
  Incompatible generators (validateGenerationRequest against the lobby's own
  size/colony count) are shown disabled with their reason instead of being
  hidden or silently failing to generate.
- CustomGamePreferences persists the chosen sort order (wire format bumped
  to version 2, with a tested version-1 fallback to Random).

Tested: full custom-setup-test suite (incl. the landscape-picker interaction
harness and a new preferences round-trip/backward-compat check) and the
macOS arm64 map-generator-golden-test both pass; the golden fingerprints are
byte-identical, confirming the tag/registry change has no effect on
generated output.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Rework: colocate generator tags in each generator's own file, not a table

Per review feedback ("don't centralize the tags... doesn't scale nicely as
we try add more generators"): dropped the centralized GeneratorTags.h/.cpp
lookup table entirely. Each generator's ...Definition() now sets its own
GeneratorDefinition::tags field directly, alongside its controls/revision/
validateWorld/etc, the same way every other registration field already
works. Touches all 49 playable generators plus Uniform; the tag values
themselves are unchanged from the previous commit, just relocated.

GeneratorRegistry's constructor keeps requiring every non-editor-only
generator to have a non-empty tags field, now reading it directly off the
definition instead of filling it in from a lookup. LandscapePickerScreen's
filter-category/value derivation now scans the entries it was actually
given (each carrying its generator's own tags) instead of calling into the
removed table.

Re-validated after the move: build clean, map-generator-golden-test
macos-arm64 still 424/424 byte-identical (tag relocation has no effect on
generated output), and the full custom-setup-test suite still passes
(including the landscape-picker interaction harness and the preferences
round-trip/backward-compat checks added earlier).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Fix landscape picker: true random reshuffle, fixed card size, self-narrowing
filters, inline size/colony controls, and a visual re-derivation of tags

Six pieces of testing feedback on the previous two passes, addressed together:

1. Random sort order was static: it fell through to the registry's own
   catalog order (shuffled once, fixed forever) instead of drawing a new
   permutation every time the dialog opened. rebuild() now shuffles with
   std::mt19937 seeded from std::random_device whenever SortOrder::Random is
   active, so every open (and every return to Random from Alphabetical)
   reshuffles for real; Alphabetical stays deterministic. Proven, not just
   asserted: a new landscapeRandomOrder() harness check constructs two
   sheets on the same entries and requires their orders differ from each
   other and from the untouched catalog order.

2. A single filtered-down result stretched to fill the whole grid width.
   Card/column count is now sized purely from the sheet's own width, never
   clamped down to how many results are currently visible - a lone match
   sits at its normal size in an otherwise-empty grid.

3. Picking filters could walk you into a dead end (every option shown, zero
   maps left). Each category's dropdown now offers only the values that
   still leave at least one result once every OTHER active filter is
   applied (matchesFilters(index, skip)), with a live count per option and
   for "Any", faceted-search style - picking any shown option can no longer
   empty the sheet.

4. Map size and colony count are now editable right on the picker (three
   shared-control dropdowns, reusing GenerationRequest::sharedControls()),
   not only inherited read-only from the lobby behind it. Changing any of
   them (setShared) rewrites every entry's request, recomputes which
   generators are still compatible, and rerolls every visible preview
   immediately - fast comparison across the whole grid, not a per-map edit
   - and CustomGameScreen reads the picker's final size/count back on any
   exit (confirmed or cancelled) to keep its own setup in sync, the same
   two-way relationship the sort order already has.

5. The preview widget's own scroll-to-zoom competed with scrolling the
   list. Scroll wheel is no longer forwarded to a tile's MapPreview on this
   screen at all; it is always grid scrolling here. (Drag-to-pan and
   double-click-to-reset on a preview are untouched.)

6. Tag re-derivation from the actual rendered maps (report was: repeated-
   wedge under-applied - "a lot more maps use rotational symmetry than
   this"). Generated and visually inspected whole-map previews (via the
   game's own generator + render_terrain.py) for every playable generator
   rather than re-reading code/docs. Findings, starting with the checkpoint
   category:
   - fairness:repeated-wedge added to city-states, carousel, coral,
     amphitheatre, switchbacks, lava-shield, fjord-continent and emoji -
     each renders an unmistakable pie-slice/pinwheel layout around one
     shared centre and had no fairness tag at all before this pass.
   - A second fairness value, stamped-lattice, introduced for the
     different pattern the quarter-turn-stencil generators actually show:
     an identical module repeated on a translational lattice with no
     shared centre (forts, glacis, bajada, allotments, caravanserai,
     karst-towers, hills) - visually distinct from repeated-wedge and was
     being missed by that tag entirely.
   - terrain:novelty added to continents: this build's atlas renders as a
     recognisable real coastline (Australia/New Zealand), the same kind of
     signature Emoji's drawn shapes are tagged novelty for, not a
     landscape designed for play (per review feedback).
   - everglades' style:wide-open removed: the rendered map is nearly
     wall-to-wall pools, the opposite of open ground; left without a style
     tag rather than guessing a replacement.
   - Spot-checked and left unchanged where the existing tags already
     matched the image: contested-commons and canals (no shared-centre or
     lattice symmetry visible - scattered/grid, correctly untagged for
     fairness), symmetric-arena and sierpinski-gardens (already
     exact-symmetry), tidal-flats and spider-web (already repeated-wedge),
     hilbert-river and old-town (no symmetry claim, correctly untagged).
   This was a representative pass (~30 of 49 generators individually
   re-viewed against their rendered previews), not an exhaustive one; an
   independent reviewer is going over the full tag set against the
   rendered images separately.

Re-validated after all six changes together: build clean: full
custom-setup-test suite passes, including the new random-order check and
the existing landscape-picker interaction harness; map-generator-golden-test
macos-arm64 still 424/424 byte-identical (none of this touches generation
output).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Randomize the landscape picker's order once per run, not on every rebuild

Refines the previous fix. FEEDBACK 2026-09-17 after trying it live: "I don't
like how the random order changes sometimes while I'm using the UI. Maybe
the random order should be randomized once when the app starts and then
stays consistent for the duration of execution." The prior fix drew a fresh
std::mt19937/random_device shuffle inside rebuild() itself, so cards visibly
reordered on every filter/sort touch within one dialog session, not just on
each fresh open - too unstable to browse against.

randomOrderFor(count) now draws that shuffle at most once per process run
per distinct entry count (a function-local static cache), and rebuild()
applies that fixed permutation, narrowed to whatever the active filters
still allow, without disturbing the relative order of what remains -
mirroring how Alphabetical's stable_sort already relates filtering to
order. Relaunching the app draws a new permutation; nothing that happens
inside one run's dialog (reopening it, touching a filter, switching back
from Alphabetical) does.

Flipped the assertions in landscapeRandomOrder() to match: two sheets
built in the same process now must land on the SAME order (proving
stability within a run) while still not being the untouched catalog order
(proving it is a real shuffle, not the old fallthrough); added a check
that filtering and un-filtering a third sheet returns to that identical
order rather than redrawing it.

Re-validated: build clean, full custom-setup-test suite passes (including
the updated random-order check), map-generator-golden-test macos-arm64
still 424/424 byte-identical.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Sonnet 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

FEEDBACK 2026-09-17: "the error messages showing why a map can't generate,

Follow-up: "because otherwise its getting cutoff and ellipsed" - the old

Re-validated what could run: build clean, full custom-setup-test suite
passes, map-generator-golden-test macos-arm64 still 424/424 byte-identical.

* Never leave an enabled card's preview square blank while it rolls

Investigated a report of a few completely blank cards (no name, no image,
no reason) in a screenshot taken at an unusual size (64x128, 2 colonies) -
an aspect ratio only easily reachable now via the new inline size/colony
controls, right after they trigger setShared()'s full reroll of every card.

Swept every playable generator's actual --generate-map behaviour at that
exact width/height/colony combination first, to rule out a silent
validation/generation gap: every one of them either completes or is
rejected up front with a proper, non-empty reason (e.g. "Lava shield needs
128-512 tile sides and an aspect ratio no greater than 2:1") - no hangs, no
empty diagnostics. So the disabled-card path (name + reason, now relocated
into the square) was never the source of a truly blank card; that part of
the pipeline is sound.

preview is still Pending or Generating (normal immediately after opening
the sheet, and especially right after setShared() resets every card at

commits.subject: Fix scons bundle: stale binary path, missing codesign, dropped dylibs (#335)
commits.body:
scons release=1 bundle has been broken in three separate ways, all
surfaced by actually trying it end to end today:

- It still pointed at src/glob2 from before the project moved to an
  out-of-tree build/ directory, so it silently packaged an empty
  Contents/MacOS.
- It never code-signed anything. Harmless on old Intel Macs, but
  install_name_tool (used to rewrite bundled libraries' load commands)
  invalidates a Mach-O's existing signature, and Apple Silicon's
  kernel kills any process holding a page with an invalid one.
- Its dependency walker only resolved absolute (/opt/homebrew/...)
  library paths. Three Homebrew dylibs declare their own dependencies
  via bare @rpath/ or @loader_path/ entries instead (boost's
  container/date_time pair, libwebp's libsharpyuv and libjxl_cms);
  their references got rewritten to point into the bundle but the
  actual files were never copied there, so the app died at launch
  with "Library not loaded" the moment any of those codepaths ran.

Fixes: point BUNDLE_BINARIES at the real build output; resolve
@rpath//@loader_path/ entries by searching Homebrew's lib and Cellar
directories the same way an absolute path is resolved, so nothing is
silently dropped; sign every bundled library and binary after
install_name_tool touches it, then sign the assembled bundle itself.
Also registered an Alias so `scons bundle` reports success instead of
scons additionally trying (and failing) to resolve "bundle" as a
literal file target, even though the bundle it built was fine.

Verified with a full clean `scons release=1 bundle`: exits 0, and the
resulting Glob2.app launches with no crash report (previously
SIGKILL'd immediately with a CODESIGNING/"Invalid Page" exception).
The everyday `scons release=1 build/src/glob2` dev build is untouched.

commits.subject: Landscape picker: second tag pass from an independent visual review (#336)
commits.body:
Re-derived generator tags from rendered previews again, this time acting on
an independent reviewer's pass over the first batch (#333). No generation
logic changed - tags only.

Stamped-lattice additions (translational repeat, no shared centre), high
confidence from the reviewer plus my own render check: Ring World (belt's
start-bearing stretches are periodic along its length), Polder, Old Growth,
Breachable Highlands, Hedgerow Country, Rice Terraces, Plantations. Also
added it to two the reviewer flagged as lower-confidence but that read
unambiguously once rendered: Drumlin Field (aligned parallel rows of
islands) and Locust (its circle/square oases repeat on an obvious grid) -
and to Rain Shadow, whose parallel ridge-valley bands use the same repeated-
module mechanism as Bajada (already tagged). Left Canals alone: its own
comment says the canal grid is deliberately warped into irregular blocks
and fairness comes from picking the two blocks farthest apart on the block
graph, not from identical repeated modules - forcing stamped-lattice on it
would misdescribe the mechanism.

Terrain/feature corrections against rendered previews:
- Concrete Islands: terrain:natural -> terrain:novelty (sharp deliberate
  rectangles/triangles, not an eroded coastline); feature:ocean ->
  feature:canals (no open ocean in a render - the water is the channels).
- City States: feature:canals/feature:islands -> feature:stone-walls (the
  wedge dividers are stone roads and walls; no canals, no separate islands).
- Anthill: terrain:arena -> terrain:natural (an organic tunnel network, not
  a constructed battle arena).
- Old Town: feature:plazas -> feature:lakes (the open spots are ponds).
- Honeycomb Isle: added terrain:novelty alongside terrain:urban (the hex
  tiling itself reads as stylised on top of the urban ruins).
- Sierpinski Gardens: dropped feature:canals (the nested squares are lakes
  per the generator's own lakeIn/wheatShore code; connectors are sand
  paths, not water).
- Tidal Flats: feature:ocean -> a new feature:tidal (the background is
  exposed sand/mud, not open water - checked the other 8 feature:ocean
  users and they're all genuine open-water maps, so this wasn't overload,
  just two real mismatches).
- River: reviewer asked me to verify feature:river directly; re-rendered at
  the seed the code comment describes (256x256, seed 3) and it shows one
  clear winding channel splitting the map into banks, so no change.

Vocabulary policy calls:
- terrain:arena had two meanings: a single shared, contested battleground
  (Carousel, Amphitheatre, Symmetric Arena, Spider Web, Switchbacks, Maze -
  all paired with repeated-wedge/exact-symmetry fairness) vs. a lattice of
  separate walled compounds, one per colony (Forts, Breachable Highlands -
  both paired with stamped-lattice fairness). The fairness tag already
  present tracked this split almost perfectly, so introduced terrain:
  stronghold for the second group and reserved terrain:arena for the first.
- feature:mountains and style:expansion: left alone. Checked every user of
  each - the mountains tag is independently earned by six generators with
  genuinely different mountain treatments, and style:expansion (Old Growth,
  Locust) describes a distinct dynamic from style:sprawling (pushing back
  hostile terrain from a small enclosed start vs. spreading across an
  already-open map) - narrow, correctly-scoped vocabulary, not a defect.

Validation: rebuilt clean; MapGeneratorGoldenTest macos-arm64 (424 rows, 0
failures, as expected for tag-only changes); CustomGameSetupHarness full
suite (ALL CUSTOM SETUP TESTS PASSED).

commits.subject: Fix scons bundle: bundle SDL3 for sdl2-compat's runtime dlopen (#337)
commits.body:
The #335 bundle fix resolved static (LC_LOAD_DYLIB) dependencies, but
Homebrew's sdl2 formula is now just an alias for sdl2-compat, a shim
that wraps SDL3 and dlopen()s libSDL3.dylib by relative name
(@loader_path/libSDL3.dylib, among others) the first time SDL
initializes, instead of declaring it as a normal linked dependency.
otool -L can never see that, so the dependency walker never copied
SDL3 into the bundle, and sdl2-compat aborted in its own startup
constructor before glob2's own code ever ran (SIGABRT, no crash
report useful beyond "abort() called" and a dyld-initializer frame in
libSDL2-2.0.0.dylib).

Fixes: added a small table of known runtime dlopen() dependencies to
addDependentLibsToBundle.py (currently just SDL2 -> SDL3) that get
resolved and bundled alongside the normal static-dependency walk.

Verified with a full clean scons release=1 bundle: libSDL3.dylib and
libSDL3.0.dylib are now present and signed in Contents/Frameworks, and
the resulting Glob2.app launches and stays running with no crash
report, both standalone and after installing into /Applications.

commits.subject: Add the Hidden Oasis map generator (#338)
commits.body:
* Add the Hidden Oasis map generator

Dry canyon country round a sandstone plateau that hides the map's only
algae. One winding gorge is the only way in, and every colony starts with a
level-1 tower over a pinch of it, on a ledge behind two tiles of rock at the
head of its own box canyon. Every canyon runs forwards to the mouth's cliff,
so Central Quarry's walk-band search on the walk to the mouth is fair for
every tower's door as well. A granted level-0 school (a toggle, on by
default) keeps AI games from running at level 0 behind a seal no AI breaks.

Shared code: Central Quarry's site search, territory flood, trail opener,
sealed garden, field trimming, wheat top-up, sliver removal and spline path
move to shared/, with Karst towers' design cache. reachFrom is a bounded
flood that costs what it reaches rather than the map. BiomeKit gains
optional per-100000 outcrop and grove counts so a resource amount has no
dead steps. Every other generator's golden rows are unchanged.

Three rounds of independent review, 48 AI games, a 975-map control study,
2,000 random requests with no validation failure, profiling (about a
quarter less CPU a map), translations in every catalog reviewed by a
separate agent, macOS golden rows. See docs/map-generators/HIDDEN_OASIS.md.

commits.subject: Add experimental Even Ground and Marchland map generators (#345)
commits.body:
* Add Equilibrium, a map generator that solves for terrain instead of drawing it

Every landscape in the catalog picks a shape and then works to make that shape
fair. Equilibrium states what the finished map must be true of -- equal
walking-distance-decayed catchments per colony, everyone connected, building
room at every home, a requested route width -- and anneals a coarse lattice
until it satisfies them. The terrain is the output of the constraints.

Two passes, each preserving its own budget so the sliders set quantities the
search may place but not change: a shape pass swapping water with land, and a
cheap stock pass swapping crops between land cells. The stock pass is the one
that buys the fairness, cutting catchment spread about sixty-fold.

Measured against the existing landscapes on the report's canonical fairness
(16 seeds, 256x256, four colonies): 0.930 against Watershed's 0.824 and
Continents' 0.796, level with Rain shadow, short of Savannah's 0.940 and well
short of exact symmetry. EQUILIBRIUM.md records that, the four formulations
that failed on the way -- speckled water, featureless uniformity, plantable
doorsteps, and a balance slider that measurably did nothing -- and what has not
been tested: no AI games, no tournament, one platform.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add Tug: drawn country from the shared toolkit, with one solved decision

Homelands of farmed country parted by a dry march nobody can build on, and a
rope of prizes strung through it -- the only fruit on the map, each with a
quarry, each on a clearing of living ground. Territory never moves; only the
rope does.

Almost all of it is drawn with primitives that already exist, because
construction reaches these properties and a search would be a worse way to get
them: growTerritories for equal ground, separateTerritories for the march,
farthestSites plus recentreSites for the homes, regionHome for the swarms, and
growLakeBeside to give every colony a private lake of exactly the same size.

One decision is solved, because construction cannot reach it: which sites in the
march become the prizes. That is a constraint over an N-colony by K-prize matrix
of walking costs on asymmetric ground, scored with the engine's own cost model.
It is also nearly free -- each colony's cost field is flooded once, so a move is
a table lookup.

The levelling slider turns the search off so its worth is measurable rather than
asserted. A rope dealt at random and left alone misses the contested-prize bar on
16 seeds out of 16; with the search it holds on all of them, cutting the contest
gap from 32 walking steps to 3. TUG.md records that, the two promises that were
mis-stated before this one (per-prize equidistance is over-constrained, equal
mean walk measures the map's shape rather than the rope), the solid-grove wall
and the anti-correlated crop fields, and what is untested: no AI games, no
tournament, one platform.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Repair the contract header's merge when stacking Tug on Equilibrium

Rebasing Tug onto Equilibrium conflicts in every file the two generators both
add an entry to. A union is the right resolution for the registry, the source
list, the catalog, the golden table and the translation tables -- each gains one
independent entry per generator -- but it is the wrong one for a C++ header,
where it spliced tugContracts() into the middle of equilibriumContracts() and
left the file unparseable. This is the failure the framework doc warns about.

Rebuilt that file the way the doc prescribes instead: take one branch's version
whole and re-apply the other's purely additive function as a patch.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Extract a shared constraint-solving module and put both maps on it

Equilibrium and Tug had grown the same machinery independently: a Metropolis
loop, a geometric cooling schedule, deterministic draws from a named stream, and
a measure of how unequally something is shared between colonies. shared/Solve.h
is that, once, with the propose/cost/undo shape all three of their passes fit.

Standardising the report is what made it worth doing. The module records the
cost with and without the search for every run, and reading that back showed
Equilibrium's shape pass finishing at a WORSE cost than it started on five seeds
in twelve -- annealing ends wherever its last accepted move left it, which on a
schedule slightly too warm at the end is not the best place it visited. That was
invisible while each map reported only its own residuals.

So the module keeps the best arrangement it sees and returns that, through
optional remember/recall callbacks. The shape pass now ends worse on none of
twelve seeds, and its median cost falls 2.756 -> 1.646 rather than -> 1.732.

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table; the refactor changes no existing
map. Both generators' maps do change, since the shared loop draws in a
different order.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Wrap Solve.h's comments to the repository's 100 columns

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Name the objective's terms, and give Tug a commons instead of parcels

Two things, both of which came out of being able to see which constraint was
actually binding.

Solve.h gains Objective: a cost built from named weighted terms that reports
each term's residual to telemetry. Storage is inline so the hot loop uses the
same code that reports, and there is no second copy of the weights to drift.

Reading that back immediately found a bad target in Equilibrium. Its shoreline
term was set to 0.8 and the ground cannot reach it -- at a tenth of the map under
water the shoreline settles near 1.3 -- so the term contributed about seventy per
cent of the shape cost while never shrinking, drowning out every target that
could be improved. Setting it to what is reachable lifted canonical fairness
0.889 -> 0.916 and the worst colony 0.186 -> 0.230, the best it has measured.
Equilibrium also gains an approach-parity term (equal open ground on the ring a
rival arrives across, its only word about defensibility) and a field-clustering
target, which gathers the same crop budget into belts instead of the confetti the
previews showed.

Tug stops sharing the whole map out. Each colony keeps the nearest 45 per cent of
its fair share and the rest is commons: buildable ground with its own crops and
wood, where expansion, battlefields and the rope all live. The sand shrinks from
"everything unowned" -- which meant there was nowhere on the map to expand into
at all -- to a thin collar that only stops a farm creeping out of its country.
Its homelands are also jostled off the lattice farthestSites leaves them on: an
equal-area partition of a torus from maximally-spread seeds is a 2x2 grid, which
is why the marches read as city streets, and no border cost fixes that.

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Wrap Objective's comment to 100 columns

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Draw each seed's targets, so a solved map stops repeating itself

A constraint solver with fixed targets hands every seed the identical problem,
and a search is very good at finding the same answer to the same question: the
layout moves about but the character never does, which is why twelve seeds of
Equilibrium looked like twelve photographs of one map. The one target that was
already drawn per seed -- its water-body count -- was also the only thing
producing visible seed-to-seed difference, which was the clue.

Solve.h gains drawnTarget, and both maps now solve a brief rather than a
constant. Equilibrium draws its shoreline and field-clustering targets; Tug
draws how much of the country the colonies keep and how densely they farm it, so
one seed is islands of farm in a wide commons and the next is neighbours with a
march between them. Every drawn target is reported, so an odd seed can be read
as what it was asked for rather than as a search that failed.

Tug's collar also widens and its homeland farming is drawn well above the
commons' fixed light share, which is what should tell a colony's own country
from open ground at a glance.

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Let each seed choose which optional targets it solves to

Drawing a target's value widens a map's character; dropping the target widens it
much further, because a term that is off is not a weak preference but permission
to do anything else in that dimension. Solve.h gains Emphases: a named set of
optional targets, of which each seed draws some and ignores the rest, reported so
an unusual map reads as the brief it solved rather than a search gone wrong.

The distinction that makes it safe is between invariants and character. Every
colony joined to the rest, ground to build on, a crop within reach and equal
catchments are not character; a seed that switched one off would be broken rather
than varied. Only the character terms go in the draw.

Approach parity was in that set at first and should not have been: it says every
colony is as exposed as every other, which is fairness wearing character's
clothes. Measured over twelve seeds, putting it up for the draw cost a median
fairness of 0.879 and a worst colony of 0.146; taking it back out recovered
0.897 and 0.221, against 0.916 and 0.230 for the fixed-target version it
replaces. So the variety is not free -- it buys a wider range of maps for a small
and now-understood amount of balance, and the spread across seeds is much wider
at both ends (0.837 to 0.981).

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Draw each seed's composition, not only its targets and arrangement

The variety was never in the targets. Every target could be drawn per seed and
every arrangement searched, and twelve seeds still came out with water between
8.2 and 8.9 per cent of the map and wheat between 4.7 and 5.1, because the
budgets were exact and only their arrangement was ever in question: each seed was
the same country rearranged. Rearrangement is a weak lever on how a map looks.

So a seed now draws its own weather. Equilibrium's water and crop budgets are
drawn round what the sliders asked for rather than taken from them, which widens
the water across twelve seeds from a spread of 0.7 points to 13.1 and the wheat
from 0.4 to 5.5 -- one seed is lake country and the next dry downland, which is
visible at a glance in a way none of the earlier work was. A slider is now the
middle of a band rather than a figure; what it still promises is its direction.

Fairness terms also go into the per-seed draw now, approach parity among them, on
the explicit steer that variety matters more here than an even contest. Median
fairness falls 0.889 -> 0.870 and its spread across seeds widens to 0.81..0.94.
Playability is not in the draw and never will be: every colony joined to the
rest, with ground to build on and a crop within reach, is what makes the result a
map rather than what gives it a character.

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Fray the homeland edge, and record why it is square in the first place

The square sand outlines on every Tug map were never the collar's doing. A
homeland is bounded by taking a colony's nearest tiles by walk, the walk is
eight-connected, and eight-connected distance is the Chebyshev metric - whose
balls are squares. The collar is dilated round that, so it inherits the shape.

Ranking the tiles by the walk bent with a noise field frays that edge, and the
swing is drawn per seed so one seed's homelands are compact and the next's follow
the ground. It took two goes: bending it with the relief field did almost nothing
because relief undulates about every forty tiles and a homeland is sixty across,
so over that span it is nearly a gradient and slid the square sideways rather
than breaking up its edge. An edge frays at the scale of the fraying.

What this does not do is make the homelands organic. A frayed square is still a
square, and it will stay one while the ranking is a distance ball: the fix for

* Draw the river, search only where to put it

A landform is the case that does not fit "state the target and let the solver
find it", and working out why sharpened the rule the rest of this branch runs on.

Asking a solver for water in the middle of the map does not produce a river. A
positional target is met just as well by a blob, a ring or a scatter of ponds
with the right centre-weighted share - nothing in such a measure selects for
thin, long or joined-up. Tighten it until only a one-cell band satisfies it and
a channel does appear, ruler-straight at a fixed offset, because a band is the
only shape the measure named; making it meander means describing the meander,
and then the route is drawn and the search has coloured it in.

The deeper reason is the shape of the landscape. Every target these maps solve
well is statistical - a share, a ratio, a count, a spread - and those have
gradients. "One joined-up channel crossing the map" is topological, and those
are needles: nine tenths of a river is a lake and a pond and scores no better
than one tenth of one, so there is nothing to descend.

So shared/Rivers.h draws the bed - a closed wandering loop across the torus,
joined up and the right width by construction, its meander a sum of harmonics
periodic over the crossing so the loop closes with no seam, taking its draws
from a named stream so it replays from the seed. Tug then scores fourteen
candidate beds on the part construction cannot settle: keeping out of the towns,
touching the homelands evenly, lying in the commons, and putting the colonies on
both banks. Fourteen candidates is an exhaustive loop, not an annealing run;
searching there would be the same mistake in the other direction. Crossings
split the same way - that the country stays in one piece is an invariant, so
fordsToRejoin guarantees it by construction, while how many more fords there are
is character.

Three things measurement caught that reading the code did not:

- Scoring the homelands with imbalance() inverted the best case. It reads
  all-zero shares as "every claimant has none of a thing it needs" and charges a
  point, which is right for wheat and exactly wrong for water nobody wanted: a
  bed touching no farm at all scored the worst possible 40, and the choice fell
  to the other terms. Only ask how evenly the water fell once some has fallen.
- Forded only where connectivity demanded, the bed was a wall. At 512x512 it
  left one colony contesting five prizes and another one, failing this map's own
  rope check. Two crossings per colony, spread along the bed, is what makes it
  route a war instead of stopping one.
- The first beds read as canals. A wander of 0.17 of the crossed side over 256
  tiles is nearly a ruled line - the very failure the header argues a positional
  constraint would give. 0.30 with a fourth harmonic reads as a river on most
  seeds, and costs one seed in 24.

Where the gate sits is measured, not chosen. The bed that broke the rope ran
0.42 of its length in the commons; every bed at 0.63 and above made a valid map;
0.60 keeps clear of the failure without turning away the beds that were fine.
Crowded country simply gets no river, which is honest rather than a shortfall: a
landform is character, and a seed may have none. Over 24 seeds at 256x256, 11
asked for a river and 5 got one.

* Stop rebuilding one clearance field per colony, and drop the heap for buckets

Equilibrium is the slowest generator in the catalog by a wide margin - 288 ms a map
against 174 for the next one, about 9 per cent of the whole catalog's generation time -
so it is where profiling starts. Sampling 400 maps at 256x256 with four colonies put
almost all of it in scoreShape, the shape pass's cost function, which runs once per
annealing proposal. Two things in it were waste, and neither changes a single map:
456 golden rows and all 17 contract suites are unchanged.

First, scoreShape asked widestWalkClearance for each colony's way out, and that
function begins by computing clearance(t, mask) - a full distance transform of the
land. The field depends on nothing but the mask, which is the same for every colony, so
a four-colony map built it four times a proposal and an eight-colony map eight times.
It was 30 per cent of the generator's run time. There is now an overload taking a
precomputed field, and the caller computes it once; clearance fell from 4614 samples to
1391. The old signature stays for the validators that ask a single question.

Second, what was left on top was the widest-path search's own priority queue, with two
fifths of its time inside __pop_heap. The keys are clearances - small bounded integers,
at most half the shorter side - so a comparison heap is the wrong structure. A bucket
per width walked from the widest down gives the same visit order at O(1) a push and a
pop, and touches a flat vector instead of sifting a growing array. It is correct for
the same reason Dijkstra is: relaxation only ever produces min(width, room), which
cannot exceed the bucket being drained, so the first pop of a tile is final.

Also lifts the three map-sized buffers scoreShape allocated on every proposal onto the
Shape scratch that already existed for the walk queue.

Generation time for Equilibrium, measured with the golden test's telemetry mode, mean
of three seeds at 256x256 with four colonies:

  before             297.8 ms
  clearance hoisted  239.2 ms   -19.7%
  bucket queue       210.7 ms   -29.3% overall

Wall clock for 20 maps end to end: 5.93 s to 4.82 s at 256x256 with four colonies, and
5.45 s to 4.20 s for three maps at 512x512 with eight colonies and Patient effort, where
there are eight redundant transforms a proposal rather than four.

* Read the walk field once per cell, where aliasing stopped the compiler doing it

Two loops in Equilibrium's shape pass reload values the compiler is not allowed to
assume are stable, because in both cases the reads and the writes are through vectors
it cannot prove disjoint.

walkLand wrote steps[next] = steps[i] + 1 inside the neighbour loop, so steps[i] was
reloaded on each of the four steps even though it cannot change: a cell is written only
while still unvisited, and this one has been dequeued. The scoring loop was worse - it
indexed s.walk[k][i] four times a cell and accumulated straight into three vector
elements, so the step count and all three running totals went back to memory every
iteration.

Both now read into locals. No map moves: 456 golden rows and 17 contract suites
unchanged.

Equilibrium's generation time, mean of three seeds at 256x256 with four colonies:

  before this branch's profiling   297.8 ms
  clearance hoisted out of the loop 239.2 ms
  bucket queue for the widest walk  210.7 ms
  these two loops                   193.0 ms   -35.2% overall

Worth recording what is NOT the problem, so nobody looks again: cache. The search runs
on a 32x32 lattice, so a walk field is 4 KB, the whole per-proposal working set about
25 KB, and it sits in L1 throughout - shrinking the step counts to int16 would buy
nothing. Torus::at already takes a compare rather than two divisions on the common
in-range step. What is left is real work: four breadth-first walks and one widest-path
search per proposal, now about 36 per cent each of the pass.

* Write up what the solved maps taught, as a reference for the next one

A new references/constraint-solving.md in the map-design skill, and edits where the
existing guidance is now wrong or incomplete.

The reference leads with the result rather than the machinery, because the result is
the useful part: two generators built as a deliberate pair, one searching the whole
terrain and one searching a single decision, score the same statically (0.894 against
0.890) and disagree completely in games - the narrow one passes a fairness tournament
and the broad one fails it, 25.9 pp of position bias with one start winning eight
games out of eight. So the three conditions for writing a search at all, and a bias
towards aiming it at fewer decisions than feels natural.

Then the things that cost time here:

  - optimise what decides games, not what is easy to measure. Even Ground drove its
    catchment spread to near zero and never had colony fitness - the measure that
    actually predicts wins - in its objective at all. Its own per-colony telemetry
    said so before the tournament did, and nobody had read it.
  - statistical targets have gradients; topological ones are needles. The river is the
    worked example, including why a positional target yields a ruler-straight channel,
    and the rule it produced: draw the landform, search its placement.
  - invariants are guaranteed by construction and never appear in the cost function;
    character is what a seed draws.
  - draw the brief per seed or every seed is the same map.
  - name the objective's terms - it is what found a term contributing a constant 8.000
    on every seed, and an inverted one scoring the best case worst.
  - annealing practicalities: keep the best state, heat in the cost's units, spend a
    fairness slider on the pass that is cheap to re-score.
  - a stream name is part of every draw, so rename before the measurement pass. This
    bit twice in one afternoon, once silently.
  - refuse early with advice rather than failing late, with the method for setting the
    threshold from measured failure rates.
  - making a cost function fast, and checking whether cache is the problem before
    optimising for it - here it was not, the working set was 25 KB.
  - the verification ladder, cheapest first, ending at the tournament, which is the
    only rung that caught the real defect.

Plus a checklist.

Edits elsewhere: SKILL.md gains the read-this-when line and a note that a searched
fairness score is the weakest evidence of fairness there is, since the search drove
the number it was given; the verification step now says to finalise stream and key
names before measuring; the tuning playbook says to weight the tournament more heavily
when a generator optimises fairness, not less; and implementation-and-verification
records the split the rename accidentally demonstrated - golden rows say nothing
changed, contracts say the design still holds, and all 17 contracts survived every map

commits.subject: Add Bastion Keys swimming-only island forts and map-making lessons (#354)
commits.body:
* Add Equilibrium, a map generator that solves for terrain instead of drawing it

Every landscape in the catalog picks a shape and then works to make that shape
fair. Equilibrium states what the finished map must be true of -- equal
walking-distance-decayed catchments per colony, everyone connected, building
room at every home, a requested route width -- and anneals a coarse lattice
until it satisfies them. The terrain is the output of the constraints.

Two passes, each preserving its own budget so the sliders set quantities the
search may place but not change: a shape pass swapping water with land, and a
cheap stock pass swapping crops between land cells. The stock pass is the one
that buys the fairness, cutting catchment spread about sixty-fold.

Measured against the existing landscapes on the report's canonical fairness
(16 seeds, 256x256, four colonies): 0.930 against Watershed's 0.824 and
Continents' 0.796, level with Rain shadow, short of Savannah's 0.940 and well
short of exact symmetry. EQUILIBRIUM.md records that, the four formulations
that failed on the way -- speckled water, featureless uniformity, plantable
doorsteps, and a balance slider that measurably did nothing -- and what has not
been tested: no AI games, no tournament, one platform.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Add Tug: drawn country from the shared toolkit, with one solved decision

Homelands of farmed country parted by a dry march nobody can build on, and a
rope of prizes strung through it -- the only fruit on the map, each with a
quarry, each on a clearing of living ground. Territory never moves; only the
rope does.

Almost all of it is drawn with primitives that already exist, because
construction reaches these properties and a search would be a worse way to get
them: growTerritories for equal ground, separateTerritories for the march,
farthestSites plus recentreSites for the homes, regionHome for the swarms, and
growLakeBeside to give every colony a private lake of exactly the same size.

One decision is solved, because construction cannot reach it: which sites in the
march become the prizes. That is a constraint over an N-colony by K-prize matrix
of walking costs on asymmetric ground, scored with the engine's own cost model.
It is also nearly free -- each colony's cost field is flooded once, so a move is
a table lookup.

The levelling slider turns the search off so its worth is measurable rather than
asserted. A rope dealt at random and left alone misses the contested-prize bar on
16 seeds out of 16; with the search it holds on all of them, cutting the contest
gap from 32 walking steps to 3. TUG.md records that, the two promises that were
mis-stated before this one (per-prize equidistance is over-constrained, equal
mean walk measures the map's shape rather than the rope), the solid-grove wall
and the anti-correlated crop fields, and what is untested: no AI games, no
tournament, one platform.

* Extract a shared constraint-solving module and put both maps on it

Equilibrium and Tug had grown the same machinery independently: a Metropolis
loop, a geometric cooling schedule, deterministic draws from a named stream, and
a measure of how unequally something is shared between colonies. shared/Solve.h
is that, once, with the propose/cost/undo shape all three of their passes fit.

Standardising the report is what made it worth doing. The module records the
cost with and without the search for every run, and reading that back showed
Equilibrium's shape pass finishing at a WORSE cost than it started on five seeds
in twelve -- annealing ends wherever its last accepted move left it, which on a
schedule slightly too warm at the end is not the best place it visited. That was
invisible while each map reported only its own residuals.

So the module keeps the best arrangement it sees and returns that, through
optional remember/recall callbacks. The shape pass now ends worse on none of
twelve seeds, and its median cost falls 2.756 -> 1.646 rather than -> 1.732.

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table; the refactor changes no existing
map. Both generators' maps do change, since the shared loop draws in a
different order.

* Wrap Solve.h's comments to the repository's 100 columns

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Name the objective's terms, and give Tug a commons instead of parcels

Two things, both of which came out of being able to see which constraint was
actually binding.

Solve.h gains Objective: a cost built from named weighted terms that reports
each term's residual to telemetry. Storage is inline so the hot loop uses the
same code that reports, and there is no second copy of the weights to drift.

Reading that back immediately found a bad target in Equilibrium. Its shoreline
term was set to 0.8 and the ground cannot reach it -- at a tenth of the map under
water the shoreline settles near 1.3 -- so the term contributed about seventy per
cent of the shape cost while never shrinking, drowning out every target that
could be improved. Setting it to what is reachable lifted canonical fairness
0.889 -> 0.916 and the worst colony 0.186 -> 0.230, the best it has measured.
Equilibrium also gains an approach-parity term (equal open ground on the ring a
rival arrives across, its only word about defensibility) and a field-clustering
target, which gathers the same crop budget into belts instead of the confetti the
previews showed.

Tug stops sharing the whole map out. Each colony keeps the nearest 45 per cent of
its fair share and the rest is commons: buildable ground with its own crops and
wood, where expansion, battlefields and the rope all live. The sand shrinks from
"everything unowned" -- which meant there was nowhere on the map to expand into
at all -- to a thin collar that only stops a farm creeping out of its country.
Its homelands are also jostled off the lattice farthestSites leaves them on: an
equal-area partition of a torus from maximally-spread seeds is a 2x2 grid, which
is why the marches read as city streets, and no border cost fixes that.

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Wrap Objective's comment to 100 columns

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Draw each seed's targets, so a solved map stops repeating itself

A constraint solver with fixed targets hands every seed the identical problem,
and a search is very good at finding the same answer to the same question: the
layout moves about but the character never does, which is why twelve seeds of
Equilibrium looked like twelve photographs of one map. The one target that was
already drawn per seed -- its water-body count -- was also the only thing
producing visible seed-to-seed difference, which was the clue.

Solve.h gains drawnTarget, and both maps now solve a brief rather than a
constant. Equilibrium draws its shoreline and field-clustering targets; Tug
draws how much of the country the colonies keep and how densely they farm it, so
one seed is islands of farm in a wide commons and the next is neighbours with a
march between them. Every drawn target is reported, so an odd seed can be read
as what it was asked for rather than as a search that failed.

Tug's collar also widens and its homeland farming is drawn well above the
commons' fixed light share, which is what should tell a colony's own country
from open ground at a glance.

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Let each seed choose which optional targets it solves to

Drawing a target's value widens a map's character; dropping the target widens it
much further, because a term that is off is not a weak preference but permission
to do anything else in that dimension. Solve.h gains Emphases: a named set of
optional targets, of which each seed draws some and ignores the rest, reported so
an unusual map reads as the brief it solved rather than a search gone wrong.

The distinction that makes it safe is between invariants and character. Every
colony joined to the rest, ground to build on, a crop within reach and equal
catchments are not character; a seed that switched one off would be broken rather
than varied. Only the character terms go in the draw.

Approach parity was in that set at first and should not have been: it says every
colony is as exposed as every other, which is fairness wearing character's
clothes. Measured over twelve seeds, putting it up for the draw cost a median
fairness of 0.879 and a worst colony of 0.146; taking it back out recovered
0.897 and 0.221, against 0.916 and 0.230 for the fixed-target version it
replaces. So the variety is not free -- it buys a wider range of maps for a small
and now-understood amount of balance, and the spread across seeds is much wider
at both ends (0.837 to 0.981).

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Draw each seed's composition, not only its targets and arrangement

The variety was never in the targets. Every target could be drawn per seed and
every arrangement searched, and twelve seeds still came out with water between
8.2 and 8.9 per cent of the map and wheat between 4.7 and 5.1, because the
budgets were exact and only their arrangement was ever in question: each seed was
the same country rearranged. Rearrangement is a weak lever on how a map looks.

So a seed now draws its own weather. Equilibrium's water and crop budgets are
drawn round what the sliders asked for rather than taken from them, which widens
the water across twelve seeds from a spread of 0.7 points to 13.1 and the wheat
from 0.4 to 5.5 -- one seed is lake country and the next dry downland, which is
visible at a glance in a way none of the earlier work was. A slider is now the
middle of a band rather than a figure; what it still promises is its direction.

Fairness terms also go into the per-seed draw now, approach parity among them, on
the explicit steer that variety matters more here than an even contest. Median
fairness falls 0.889 -> 0.870 and its spread across seeds widens to 0.81..0.94.
Playability is not in the draw and never will be: every colony joined to the
rest, with ground to build on and a crop within reach, is what makes the result a
map rather than what gives it a character.

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Fray the homeland edge, and record why it is square in the first place

The square sand outlines on every Tug map were never the collar's doing. A
homeland is bounded by taking a colony's nearest tiles by walk, the walk is
eight-connected, and eight-connected distance is the Chebyshev metric - whose
balls are squares. The collar is dilated round that, so it inherits the shape.

Ranking the tiles by the walk bent with a noise field frays that edge, and the
swing is drawn per seed so one seed's homelands are compact and the next's follow
the ground. It took two goes: bending it with the relief field did almost nothing
because relief undulates about every forty tiles and a homeland is sixty across,
so over that span it is nearly a gradient and slid the square sideways rather
than breaking up its edge. An edge frays at the scale of the fraying.

What this does not do is make the homelands organic. A frayed square is still a
square, and it will stay one while the ranking is a distance ball: the fix for
the shape itself is a different metric or a grown region, not more noise on the
edge of this one.

Only ids 58 and 59 move in the golden table.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Draw the river, search only where to put it

A landform is the case that does not fit "state the target and let the solver
find it", and working out why sharpened the rule the rest of this branch runs on.

Asking a solver for water in the middle of the map does not produce a river. A
positional target is met just as well by a blob, a ring or a scatter of ponds
with the right centre-weighted share - nothing in such a measure selects for
thin, long or joined-up. Tighten it until only a one-cell band satisfies it and
a channel does appear, ruler-straight at a fixed offset, because a band is the
only shape the measure named; making it meander means describing the meander,
and then the route is drawn and the search has coloured it in.

The deeper reason is the shape of the landscape. Every target these maps solve
well is statistical - a share, a ratio, a count, a spread - and those have
gradients. "One joined-up channel crossing the map" is topological, and those
are needles: nine tenths of a river is a lake and a pond and scores no better
than one tenth of one, so there is nothing to descend.

So shared/Rivers.h draws the bed - a closed wandering loop across the torus,
joined up and the right width by construction, its meander a sum of harmonics
periodic over the crossing so the loop closes with no seam, taking its draws
from a named stream so it replays from the seed. Tug then scores fourteen
candidate beds on the part construction cannot settle: keeping out of the towns,
touching the homelands evenly, lying in the commons, and putting the colonies on
both banks. Fourteen candidates is an exhaustive loop, not an annealing run;
searching there would be the same mistake in the other direction. Crossings
split the same way - that the country stays in one piece is an invariant, so
fordsToRejoin guarantees it by construction, while how many more fords there are
is character.

Three things measurement caught that reading the code did not:

- Scoring the homelands with imbalance() inverted the best case. It reads
  all-zero shares as "every claimant has none of a thing it needs" and charges a
  point, which is right for wheat and exactly wrong for water nobody wanted: a
  bed touching no farm at all scored the worst possible 40, and the choice fell
  to the other terms. Only ask how evenly the water fell once some has fallen.
- Forded only where connectivity demanded, the bed was a wall. At 512x512 it
  left one colony contesting five prizes and another one, failing this map's own
  rope check. Two crossings per colony, spread along the bed, is what makes it
  route a war instead of stopping one.
- The first beds read as canals. A wander of 0.17 of the crossed side over 256
  tiles is nearly a ruled line - the very failure the header argues a positional
  constraint would give. 0.30 with a fourth harmonic reads as a river on most
  seeds, and costs one seed in 24.

Where the gate sits is measured, not chosen. The bed that broke the rope ran
0.42 of its length in the commons; every bed at 0.63 and above made a valid map;
0.60 keeps clear of the failure without turning away the beds that were fine.
Crowded country simply gets no river, which is honest rather than a shortfall: a
landform is character, and a seed may have none. Over 24 seeds at 256x256, 11
asked for a river and 5 got one.

Tug's revision moves to 2: some seeds' terrain changes. 456 golden rows, 0
failures, and only id 59 moved. Contracts pass, including a new one holding the
two promises of the placement - no bed through a town, and more fords than bare
connectivity - and holding that both outcomes occur, so the emphasis is a real
draw. Telemetry: 171 cases, 0 semantic failures.

Not measured: how any of this plays. The river is a wall with fords across the
contested ground, which is exactly the kind of change that reads fine statically
and alters how a game goes. Two fords per colony is constrained only by the rope
check, not by anyone playing across one. Beds still come out near-straight when
the harmonics cancel (seed 9013).

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Close the river over the seam instead of asking strokePath to do it

Every bed came out in two pieces: a meander and a ruler-straight reach. The
straight one was not part of the river at all. strokePath works in continuous
coordinates and wraps only its writes - running past the edge is its documented
contract - so `closed` joins the last point to the first the long way, drawing a
chord back across the whole map at the offset where the bed starts and ends.

The meander is periodic over the crossing, so the point one step past the end is
exactly the first point shifted by a whole map. Stepping to it closes the loop
over the seam with an ordinary segment.

The chord was also being scored. Its tiles counted toward the bed's commons
share and its homeland intrusion, so both numbers that set kLeastCommonsShare
were measured against a shape that was never wanted. Recalibrated on clean beds:
the threshold turns out not to be a validity floor at all - 40 seeds at 0.45 and
24 at 0.40 all produce valid maps, and the golden set passes at both, including
the 512x512 case a walled march once broke, which the chord was helping to
break. What the constant actually buys is fairness, so it is now set from that:

  with a river (16 of 40)   fairness 0.871   worst -0.111
  without       (24 of 40)  fairness 0.910   worst -0.075

A bed across the contested ground is terrain one colony is nearer to, and
levelling the rope cannot buy that back. 0.45 takes a river on about four seeds
in ten for four points of a static score. The trade is deliberate and the
constant is the dial.

Rows are force-updated: revision 2 is unreleased, existing only on this branch,
so the 1->2 bump already covers this for anyone outside it. 456 rows, 0
failures, only id 59 moved; contracts pass.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Make the brief a type, and lift the river's scaffolding into the toolkit

A cleanup pass over the whole branch, aimed at the places where a convention was
doing a type's job or a stage had grown into its caller. Every step is
behaviour-preserving: both generators come out byte-identical, 456 golden rows,
0 failures, all 17 contract suites passing.

Brief (Solve.h) replaces two conventions nothing enforced. Every drawn target was
followed by a hand-written telemetry line - in all seven places the two maps drew
one - and the stream and the telemetry key were spelled separately at every call,
always as `<map>-brief` and `<map>.brief.<name>`. Two strings that must agree
were free to drift, and a forgotten line left a seed unreadable, which is exactly
the failure the drawn-target comment warns about. Holding the map's name once
makes the record a consequence of drawing. It absorbs Emphases too, since a
map's optional terms are part of the same brief, and both maps now draw the whole
brief in one place at the top of the design rather than scattering it through.

The draws keep their order within each map's stream, and streams are independent,
so the maps do not move - which the golden rows confirm rather than assume.

bestRiverAcross (Rivers.h) takes the candidate loop that was inline in Tug:
propose beds spread evenly across the map, rate each, keep the lowest. What was
Tug-specific was only ever the rating, which stays there as rateBed. The next map
that wants a river writes a scoring lambda.

Objective::residual lets a winner be read back. The bed's gate needed the commons
share and the town count of the chosen candidate, which meant three shadow
variables tracked alongside the loop and kept in step by hand. A chosen candidate
already carries every measurement that chose it, so it can just be asked.

cutRiver and rateBed come out of design(), which was 456 lines and which the
river had made worse.

Smaller: Emphases gains a default constructor so a Brief can hold one before it
draws; fordsToRejoin drops a std::function for a plain lambda.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Delete the logic that measurement says is doing nothing

A simplification pass, using the telemetry the objective terms were named for.
Every map comes out byte-identical: 456 golden rows, 0 failures, 17/17 contracts.

The split term is gone, and it is the interesting one. A river that leaves every
colony on one bank is a coastline rather than a front, so scoring it looked
obviously right. Reading what it actually came out at across the sixteen seeds
that drew a river, it was exactly 1.0 every time - because cutting a torus along
a single loop that goes all the way round leaves it connected, the way slitting
a bicycle tube along its circumference leaves a sheet. Parting a torus takes two
parallel cuts. So the term could never tell one candidate from another, and the
connectedRegions flood that computed it ran fourteen times a seed to rediscover a
constant. The golden rows confirm the reasoning: removing it moves nothing.

The recentring pass is gone. kRecentrePasses was 0, so the loop never ran - but
it sat under seven lines of comment arguing for recentring, next to a constant
switching it off. Code that cannot execute beside a comment that says it should
is worse than either alone. What remains is a note on the jostle saying why this
map deliberately has no such pass.

Emphases and drawnTarget are gone as public names, folded into Brief. Neither had
a caller outside it once Brief existed, so the module was exporting three
concepts and two explanations of the same idea. One type now.

The best-keeping-free anneal overload is gone: all three searches pass the full
five callbacks, so it was an API written for nobody. River::offset is gone,
written and never read.

None of this was load-bearing, which is the point: it accumulated a piece at a
time while tuning, and each piece looked reasonable when it went in.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Wire Tug's fruit slider, cap Equilibrium's water, and measure what a control moves

A control study over every value of every control, eight seeds each at 256x256 plus
the extremes on a small, a large and a rectangular map: 1,650 maps across the two
generators. Three things it found.

Tug's fruit-amount was not connected to anything. The prize groves were planted at a
fixed radius, so all thirteen values of the slider produced identical maps; the only
place o.fruit was read was the cramped-start relief, which rarely runs. The grove now
answers to it, scaled by area rather than by radius, because a radius scaled directly
delivers the square of what the slider asks - 300 per cent would have ringed every
prize with a nine-times grove of uncleanable fruit, exactly where the fighting is
meant to happen. scaledRadius is in Resources.h beside scaledCount, since the same
trap is there for anyone scaling a round deposit; Tug's quarry now uses it too.

Equilibrium's water-share ran to 60 per cent, and the top of that range was not a
map. Over 40 seeds at 256x256 with four colonies it refuses on 10 per cent of seeds
at 50, 15 at 55 and 20 at 60 - colonies with no wood in reach, or too few building
origins to settle - while the flood saturates near 53 per cent actual water however
much more is asked, and the 4x4 building sites fall from about 13,000 at 40 to 7,700
at 60. The range now ends at 40, where 80 seeds refuse once. The comment that said
water comes out exact is gone: the brief multiplies it by the seed's wetness, so it
sets the middle of a band, and saying otherwise was wrong.

Tug's homeland telemetry was measured before the march is opened, so widening the
march never moved it. Those two keys are now tug.territory.*, which is what they
were reading, and the homeland a colony actually keeps is counted from the finished
ground beside them - the gap between the two being what the water took.

Defaults are untouched: the eight default seeds measure identical before and after,
so the golden rows stand and revision 2 still reproduces them.

Also fixes the control study itself, which could not parse a choice control - it read
`0(Brief)` as an integer and died - so no generator with one could be studied at all.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Raise Tug's colony floor to where the late failures actually stop

The floor exists so that a request too crowded to work is refused before generating
rather than failing after, and its own comment says so. At 2600 tiles a colony it was
not doing that job. A sweep over seven shapes against 2-8 colonies found one cell that
passed the check and then failed its own validator on two thirds of seeds: 128x128
with six colonies, 2730 tiles each, almost always a homeland left with no water beside
it to regrow a crop from.

Measured per cell at ten to twelve seeds, the late-failure rate is about two thirds at
2730 tiles a colony (128x128 and 64x256 with 6, 128x256 with 12), four fifths at 2978
(128x256 with 11), and nought to a third at 3276 (128x128 with 5, 128x256 with 10) -
which is the ordinary rate the lobby's retries already cover. The floor now sits at
3000, between the two.

With that, all 196 attempts in the shape sweep either produce a valid map or are
refused up front with a reason a player can act on. Nothing generates and then fails.

The same sweep over Equilibrium puts its own late-failure rate at 9 in 384 (2.3 per
cent), all of them on 512x512 or a 4:1 rectangle and all marginal misses of the
starting-crop guarantee - 25 steps against 24. That is the rate its notes already
claimed, now measured over more cells, and is recorded rather than changed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

* Show what the controls do, in a table and a contact sheet

Both generators now carry the control study's result: a claim per control, checked as

The sheets are also there to be disagreed with. Equilibrium's ground is visibly

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
